**Sparse overlay read exploration discarded.** A temporary host-only helper synthesized zero outside current overlay bands and passed 3,000 randomized byte-slice tests with poisoned backing. It was removed with its tests: it was not integrated, and the existing evidence does not isolate full-buffer clearing as a material bottleneck. A safe implementation would also need to establish the complete draw bounds, preserve arbitrary overlay reads and screenshot reuse, and compare full-frame pixels before deployment. Use the prepared Dell timeline to measure the opportunity before adding this complexity.

**Overlay clearing is a concrete work-reduction lead.** `CaptureDesktopOverlay` in `src/kernel/src/compositor.cpp` clears the entire `width*height*4` scratch image on each overlay request before drawing the taskbar, launcher, boot summary and cursor. The recorded generation-354 3200×1800 scene therefore clears 23,040,000 bytes per capture. In the sampled no-launcher layout, the 3200×88 taskbar and 24×32 cursor bounds total about 1,129,472 bytes before band/geometry effects; this is a geometry comparison, not measured bandwidth, GPU work or an expected speedup. It is unsafe simply to skip the full clear: overlay op 2 permits arbitrary full-image reads including transparent space, and completed debug captures also overwrite the same backing buffer. A safe sparse design must preserve zero pixels outside drawn overlays, invalidate any sparse-clean state after full screenshots, allocation changes and failures, and prove all drawing stays within tracked bounds including hover, launcher, boot summary and cursor edges. Existing no-overlay experiments changed workload and did not establish a safe implementation. Use the prepared frame timeline and a pixel-equivalence oracle before attributing cost or enabling any optimized path.

**Reusable asynchronous graphics pass.** Added `graphics_pass.c/.h` and `graphics_pass.vert` to the compositor library. The pass accepts an output-sized opaque background, one clipped/scaled foreground, a distinct output DMA-BUF and optional input sync-files; it imports all three images, rejects alias/invalid geometry, records the tested graphics shader with full output coverage and no clear, submits without a CPU wait, and retains images, semaphores, framebuffer and fence until poll confirms completion. A pending or uncertain pass refuses destruction; an uncertain submission or fence status retains resources for recovery. The caller must serialize shared queue access and retain source leases/output ticket through GPU completion and OS handoff; this does not implement or relax those protocols. Physical generation-354 UID-1000 jobs `820a129fb76240cab24b735c8e110079` and `...080` passed straight/premultiplied clipped pixel oracles at 64×64 and 2560×1440 through the actual pass. Jobs `...086` and `...087` additionally verified alias and invalid-geometry rejection, rejected resubmission/destruction while pending, imported an independent producer sync-file with `GRAPHICS_PASS_IMPORT_FENCE index=0 ready=0`, checked the producer-updated first-frame pixels before reuse, then reused the same pass and verified the full second output (4,096 / 3,686,400 pixels). All four exited 0/drained. Evidence `build/hardware/dell-present-ownership-20261113/gen354-graphics-async-pass-{0,1,2,3}.json`, latest probe SHA `81db5ba49cee83a11a350a1fc7b5566d3ab16bd4546f3ab3bd3bb4e77e773dcc`, package `/nix/store/nssw7vxc4npw61diw0c25az84n2vrkvc-brook-vulkan-probe-0.1`. This is an ordinary offscreen output; the pass itself has not yet been tested with an OS-protected target, multiple passes in flight, errors/device loss or a live desktop. It supports only two layers with opaque full-size background and is not yet integrated or deployed. Normal compositor remains job `820a129fb76240cab24b735c8e110076`, PID 442/incarnation 4389. Next connect the pass to protected output and expand to actual layered scenes with compute fallback and exact identity/lease accounting before measuring visible Quake.

**Worker scheduling lead.** In the eight-frame overlap trace, nine application queue-to-take intervals had median 53.82 ms; seven overlapped a measured compositor issue-to-breadcrumb interval by roughly 31–35 ms. Some queue intervals overlap each other, so their totals cannot be summed as wall time. The retained sequence also shows a roughly 13.5 ms BCS copy between two app submissions. The current shared worker calls its BCS `service` hook before taking the next queued RCS request, while `BdwExecQueue::StartNext` selects the oldest ready request subject to owner and backing independence. These observations identify a possible scheduling tradeoff, not proof that reordering is safe or sufficient: the compositor may depend on app-owned buffers and delayed BCS affects presentation. Consider an opt-in bounded fairness experiment only after preserving per-owner/dependency order and scanout retirement, and compare game throughput, distinct compositor commits, queue ages and failure/lease behavior on the same boot. Raw events remain in `gen350-fence-compare/overlap/frame-ledger.json`.

**Dependent partial-present integration, not deployed.** Added opt-in handoff operation `BROOK_GPU_HANDOFF_RESERVE_DEPENDENT` and capability bit 4. Under the offscreen mutex it verifies the caller's nonzero last-accepted ticket before binding a scene, and records successful earlier full/partial writes into later bindings. The presenter rejects a dependent partial unless its submitted regions cover all such writes; a prior full or tracking overflow forces full fallback. Existing reservations retain the full-only guard. Recording occurs after actual presentation success but before handoff slot release, including both `PresentGopWrite` and CPU fallback in the private short-lock implementation. The renderer negotiates the capability and opt-in flag `BROOK_RENDER_EXPERIMENTAL_OVERLAP_PARTIAL`, combines pending damage footprints, passes the baseline on dependent reservations, and does not invalidate the newer displayed damage when an older ticket is discarded. Main and private renderer Nix builds passed (private `/nix/store/yq2jdp97vk2rx1mpzgrdmh0irmmh1mh9-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1`, main `/nix/store/sbh47mdhyrw9kg1jf3pyfbqf3w89aarb-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1`); the private kernel `guard-timing` target built. **Dell idle compositor tail reproduced (12 November).** Ian confirmed that only Kernel Console was visible. On the unchanged generation 308 boot `00b153f0f0eb45f081aff1bb08ca8e18`, the normal 800×500 window showed taskbar COMP p80 17 ms, p95 19 ms and max 19 ms in a completed-frame capture. Two normal → maximized → normal checks reproduced the tail. With the maximized console, the bridge reported p50 16 ms, p90 21 ms and p95 120 ms. In a steady 12.924-second maximized window the Broadwell counter advanced by 96 full presents and zero partial presents, with zero new completed console log lines. At normal size the preceding quiet control had 674 partial and zero full presents over approximately 22 seconds. After both restores the bridge p95 returned to 19 ms, and the original console layout was restored.

The renderer marks the full bounds of each visible client and its chrome as damage on every frame. A maximized window fills the desktop work area, and the taskbar overlay covers the remainder. `desktop_renderer.c` only admits a partial present when the resulting damage area is smaller than the screen. This explains the recurring full path in the maximized state. Its exact contribution to each long kernel interval remains unmeasured. The next compositor change should make window damage depend on published content and geometry, with independent checks for moves, opacity, chrome and fallback. Evidence `build/hardware/dell-compositor-tail-20261112/{idle-console-size-control.json,idle-frame/}`.

A subsequent same-boot syscall profile of `/boot/VKRENDER.ELF` PID/incarnation 53/53 located the delay in the inline present. With the normal console, 216 region presents succeeded and the longest dispatch in the handoff family was 6 ms. With the console maximized, all 16 retained slow events were successful `BROOK_GPU_HANDOFF_PRESENT_FRAME` calls of 119–127 ms. The scanout counter advanced by 120 full blits and zero partial blits across the maximized observation, and COMP p95 remained 120 ms. Zero invalid, contended or discontinuous records. The present holds the scanout and WM scene locks while waiting for the Broadwell worker. That worker revalidates the GOP backing, constructs private GPU mappings, copies the 23,040,000-byte frame into the firmware framebuffer and retires the blitter transaction before releasing ownership. The LAPIC syscall times include scheduling and the complete transaction. The relative contributions of queue wait, mapping preparation, command execution and retirement are still open. **Dell fence and cache follow-up (12 November).** The exact deployed Mesa binary resolves the repeated Quake calls to `iris_bo_wait_syncobj` at libgallium offset `0x186f6b3`. In the 41.413-second stock demo prefix on boot `1e5a6aea76484ab39b72a51190c6efb3`, there were 37,671 successful and 1,748 timed-out expired single-handle wait-all polls. Of the successful calls, 37,372 followed another success for the same handle. The Iris dependency list for each BO retains references to a private signaling syncobj shared by all BOs in a batch. The Astra-reviewed candidate records successful waits on that exact object under the existing BO dependency lock. Imported implicit sync still gets a fresh wait. The matching source checkout is `/tmp/brook-main-BrURO4`. A separate guarded kernel candidate cached the CLFLUSH capability and line size per CPU and kept the existing flush coverage, barriers and interrupt boundaries. Evidence is in `build/hardware/dell-fence-cache-20261112/`.

The cache candidate passed the guarded QEMU startup panic, reset and USB retrieval fixture, then booted on the Dell as generation 307 slot 0, payload `dell-cache-cpuid-20261112`, boot `a082d490b9ac498c8099bf2d217ee8f9`, session `7deb39bb348f4533b21fa57be7f29eca`. Generation 306 remains the known-good slot 1. The four control arms passed all 128 expected stores. With 16 MiB of extra residency, combined cache sync averaged 10.253 ms on the candidate and 10.277 ms on the previous kernel. The Intel Vulkan compute, triangle and compositor-scene oracles passed. The 0.23% difference was too small to retain the CPUID cache. The rejected patch is archived with the results. The remaining cache cost scales with the actual submitted footprint, and eliminating unused allocations requires evidence from the submitting driver.

On the same generation 307 boot, the marked 90-record Quake prefix measured 91 swaps in 47.307 seconds with stock Iris and 91 in 15.932 seconds with the patch, 1.92 to 5.71 swaps/s. Frame-interval p95 fell from 1,099 to 479 ms. Between-swap sync-object calls fell from 39,406 to 1,437 and time inside those calls from 41.614 to 2.126 seconds. Successful calls fell from 37,667 to 92. Consecutive successful polls of the same handle fell from 37,356 to zero. The process logged the exact RAM-staged Gallium path and its caller address resolved to the patched `iris_bo_wait_syncobj`. The Intel GBM/EGL independent red-clear and green-triangle checks passed. With only swap tracing, 91 swaps took 46.720 seconds stock and 14.476 seconds patched, 1.95 to 6.29/s, with p95 1,086 to 339 ms. These are app swap rates with vsync disabled.

The buildable Mesa patch is in `tools/mesa-iris-brook-pkg/`. It uses the same pinned Mesa version and matches all 107 defined dynamic symbols, SONAME and linked library names. The RAM copy uses the installed LLVM runtime path. Source-level tests covered two BOs sharing a fence, a fresh batch, mixed completed and pending dependencies, timeout retention and external implicit sync. The tests preserved independent dependencies and avoided using fence numbers to infer execution order. The permanent Dell launch path still needs selection of the patched Mesa closure. Which resident objects Quake can safely omit remains open.

**Current Dell AC firmware evidence:** Boot-pinned DSDT capture `build/hardware/dell-ac-source-dsdt-20261112/manifest.json` matches the archived 79,172-byte DSDT exactly (SHA-256 `c2e44a08eb6fc9d88229ac91f5116ace133809fef3e9090f4787fa1cc1aca56f`). `_SB.AC._PSR` reads bit 0 of EC offset 0x06 through ECR1. ECR1 uses Dell SMM while ECRD is zero. ECDV _REG selects the direct region and executes ECIN, which writes EC state and invokes firmware functions. The direct region uses the ACPI Field Lock rule. ACPICA acpiexec evaluated the live DSDT with the archived SSDTs in a host simulation, forcing ECRD=1 and initializing the simulated EC region to 0 or 1. _PSR returned the corresponding integer in each run; this tests the AML return path only. Logs are next to the DSDT capture. Brook has no AML or EC ownership implementation. Do not substitute raw port reads based on _CRS alone or replay the vendor SMI mailbox. Next resolve the EC ownership path using the firmware and a reference ACPI implementation, then validate monitor-only connected/disconnected samples on the physical machine before enabling shutdown. Post-reboot payload and durable shutdown-reason verification remain to be implemented in the host controller. Boot-supervised renderer already runs as a service. The separate debug-job supervisor case still needs a lifecycle solution.

**Render evidence review and Astra consult, 12 November:** Astra independently reviewed the rendering investigation and current source. Intel's queue admits one active request, but measured admission-lock waits were below 1 us resolution; do not assume that lock explains the latency. The older physical 23,883-page profile already showed about 30 ms cache synchronization in each direction and 50 ms device/reset, while the newer loaded renderer sample averaged roughly 19 ms sync each way and 70 ms device/reset; these wall-time stages and sample counts are not per-frame additive. Current `BdwExecSnapshotSyncForDevice/Cpu` visits every retained buffer and `BdwGpuBufferSyncCpuCache` flushes its pages without direction/dirty-range discrimination. The next bounded investigation should measure unique/repeated bytes and CPU versus elapsed sync time, split GPU issue/completion from reset/restore, and correlate producer commit/window incarnation, frame mode, queue/dependency, fence signal/observation, present and actual SAFE send including discarded offers. Separate Vulkan dispatch and barriers with matched area/layer controls; the observed 65 ms GPU bracket is not exclusive shader time. Preserve cache coherency and ownership until proven; avoid deleting flushes speculatively. Virgl's reusable contribution is generation-tagged independent ownership, dependency validation and quarantine: its measured preparation overlap still had only one outstanding request and did not show a speedup. A shared HAL alone does not enable overlap while Intel preparation and scratch state remain shared. Compare matched full/full one versus two contexts before partial/full tests.

The provider's offer-to-ACK interval alone includes time before renderer polling; the renderer only services that socket at frame entry, and presentation currently includes a CPU framebuffer copy. A shared HAL should own request identity, resources, dependencies, completion and quarantine, with independent preparation and backend-specific issue/retire; Intel's current `retainedRender` and `gemProbeTables` are shared, and virgl chunk boundaries cannot be applied to Intel batches. **Exact producer commit proof, physical trial starting:** Added owner/incarnation-checked WM begin-write and tagged-publish syscalls plus a query that returns the producer commit only for the exact still-current CPU publication generation. The async compositor now compares the captured CPU snapshot's kernel-proved commit with the last accepted direct commit, rather than assuming any later publication generation is sufficient. Untagged or stale fallback is dropped once a direct frame has been accepted. **Prevent older completed handoff frames replacing newer ones:** Added an owner-scoped successful-presentation ticket watermark to `CompositorHandoff` and enforced it in `BdwHandoffSession::PresentProbe`. Once the OS has accepted a newer output, an older ready ticket is safely retired and returns `-ESTALE` without invoking its presenter; an older in-flight ticket remains retained until completion is observed. A failed newer presentation does not advance the watermark. Owner attach resets the watermark, and committing after an owner change cannot affect the new owner. Host `test_compositor_handoff` and `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed; the latter submits two actual handoff slots via the fake worker, presents newer first, checks older remains held until observed and then cannot present, and checks a failed newer frame leaves the older one eligible. This is local only: no new Dell boot or performance gain, and it does not by itself enable concurrent desktop frames. Next retain distinct per-ticket OS scene/backdrop/chrome snapshots while the older ticket is in flight, then connect two Vulkan frame contexts and outputs with safe ordering, partial-damage dependencies, producer acknowledgements and failure recovery. **Nonblocking Vulkan frame contexts and opt-in import cache; desktop double buffering not yet wired:** Ian pointed out that the renderer waits for the preceding frame before starting the next and requested at least double buffering. `brook_vk_renderer_submit_batch_output` now submits without waiting and returns `BROOK_VK_PENDING`; `brook_vk_renderer_poll` only releases per-submission source/output imports and sync semaphores after the fence signals. A pending context cannot be reused or destroyed; an error quarantines resources. Independent contexts have independent command buffers, mapped metadata, output imports and fences. The existing desktop still uses the synchronous API: do not claim desktop double buffering. Its tracked OS scene registration requires the entire handoff session to be idle and stores only one current scene; allowing a second frame requires ticket-bound retained scene/backdrop/chrome identity, ordering of presentation and retirement, and multiple frame contexts/output buffers. Preserve OS-owned display and never release an offered producer buffer while any submitted context may read it.

**Opt-in asynchronous Intel Wayland snapshots (local, not deployed):** `BROOK_WAYLAND_INTEL_ASYNC=1` retains each producer buffer and its PRIME fd in a bounded, round-robin queue. The event loop polls the generation 202 try-CPU-read syscall instead of blocking in GEM_WAIT; while any current surface-tree image is pending, the previous published frame and frame callbacks are held. On verified readiness it copies to immutable CPU pixels, releases the producer, and repaints matching current image identities. Failed or unavailable readiness checks withhold release and disconnect the affected client; there is no blocking fallback. This is still a CPU snapshot, not direct GPU sharing, and the polling syscall's cache work can cost time. **Shared-buffer try-CPU-read syscall (local):** Added the device-neutral experimental `BROOK_SYS_GPU_BUFFER_TRY_CPU_READ` ABI in `src/shared/gpu_buffer_abi.h`, taking a retained shared-buffer fd. The guarded Intel backend returns ready after cache synchronization, `EAGAIN` without sleeping for busy producer/transition, `EIO` for uncertain/failed work, rejects CPU-protected output, and reports unsupported backends. Ready is not an ownership lease: the caller must exclude new producer writes for its whole access, and an idle buffer's cache flush still takes time proportional to its size. Normal non-guarded kernels return `ENODEV`. Guarded `syscall.cpp`, `intel_bdw_buffer.cpp` and `intel_bdw_ioctl.cpp` compiled individually using the exact existing guarded compile database into `/tmp`; an initial guarded compilation caught an undefined `EACCES` spelling and was fixed. Existing host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` covers busy, failed and successful core transition; the new userspace syscall boundary itself has not been executed. Built guest probe `/nix/store/h4a119b8crzpa7vwnb80ydj1ziwc21hv-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1/bin/brook-intel-cpu-try-test`, SHA-256 `4c5e2e51a397c25f73cfae2e6bb77e8d07637798929a3f449bc35a518697683c`, for idle, invalid arguments, unsupported fd and protected output; package checks and `git diff --check` passed. A real busy/failed producer boundary case, full guarded link/QEMU recovery gate and physical validation remain necessary. This operation is not used by Wayland yet and does not implement asynchronous commit or direct GPU sharing. No Dell image changed; generation 201 test, generation 200 rollback and SSD recovery remain.

**Intel Wayland buffer wait sampled during yquake2:** On generation 201 boot `f4e12329f20849039fbae9bf09ca85d5`, yquake2 GL3 job `4070018d6d3f4e3a97cfe131899c52b9` ran with the existing data and opened window 2/incarnation 9; close request `b673d47008aa49159aaa15b23ce297cb` completed and the game exited 0 with descendants drained. **Opt-in compact chrome sources (local, not deployed):** The renderer now supports `BROOK_RENDER_CHROME_SPANS=1`, packing the top, bottom and side chrome into separate tightly sized GPU sources instead of submitting a full-window source with transparent client interior. **Dell cache-flush instruction capability:** The measured 4.7–5.3 ms device-side and 4.8–4.9 ms CPU-side cache synchronization suggested `CLFLUSHOPT` as a possible optimization, but a direct CPUID leaf 7 subleaf 0 EBX bit 23 probe on the current Dell boot `4a0429c473f148b088b929f9c8a91800` returned `CLFLUSHOPT=0`, exit 0, descendants drained, job `ca1622808ddd4f948a6389fabaa8b640`. Transfer receipt `build/hardware/dell-clflushopt-probe-20261111/receipt.json`; probe source `/tmp/brook-cpuid-probe.c` (temporary). Brook's `/proc/cpuinfo` does not print that flag even when supported, so its absence there alone was not evidence. Intel's [optimization manual](https://cdrdv2-public.intel.com/671488/248966-Software-Optimization-Manual-V1-048.pdf) places the instruction's introduction in sixth-generation Core; this Dell reports family 6 model 61. Do not pursue CLFLUSHOPT as a Dell speedup. The existing transaction resets RCS and restores PAT after each run and requires the reset for safe retirement; replacing that behavior needs a real persistent engine owner and safe recovery, not simply removing the reset. No production code or deployed image changed.

**Oversized renderer buffers now shrink:** The Vulkan desktop's per-slot source buffers and partial output previously only grew, so a transient large window/damage region could leave subsequent submissions flushing the old high-water allocation. `source_size_policy.h` now requests recreation after 60 consecutive uses at no more than one quarter capacity, comparing page-rounded sizes; growth remains immediate, brief size changes reset the counter, and a page-sized allocation does not repeatedly shrink to itself. The renderer recreates only between completed frame attempts, keeping its existing uncertain-fence quarantine. **Broadwell scanout guard reservation (host only):** Linux i915's [primary-plane implementation](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/display/i9xx_plane.c) uses 256 KiB alignment and 128 guard PTEs for its VT-d display workaround when applicable. The unwired `BdwScanoutGgttMapping` now always aligns the visible surface to 64 pages, reserves 128 additional GGTT indices after it, and requires the backend to validate that the guard PTEs are prepared and remain valid until plane/mapping retirement. The visible mapping still uses only the protected buffer's actual pages; the reserved tail is not automatically initialized or scratch-backed. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed guard-denied/no-write, aligned protected-buffer mapping, nonoverlap with a neighboring reservation, takeover and uncertain-write retention; `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_bind` and `git diff --check` passed. This avoids an unsafe layout in the eventual hardware backend, but supplies no physical guard initialization, pin, device ownership, flip or cross-boot protection. The Dell remains on generation 190 partial with generation 189 full fallback; SSD/USB recovery unchanged.

**Protected scanout takeover and clean invalidation (host integration; not deployed):** Extended the large GGTT takeover transaction with `RetireToInvalid`, which requires all installed PTEs to match and quiescence, clears them, invalidates and checks readback; ambiguous retirement quarantines the lease. This removes scratch references after a clean retirement but does not cover a panic/reset while scanout is active. Connected the existing protected-buffer `BdwScanoutGgttMapping` adapter to a backend-provided immutable pre-takeover snapshot and scratch page, with explicit ownership validation and clear-on-retirement. Its backend remains simulated; production has no device owner, mapped PTE pages, physical flip/completion or cross-boot recovery. Fixed the transaction's reuse after successful cleanup for successive mappings; quarantined work cannot be recycled. Host `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_bind` passed scratch and invalid retirement, two-page actual accessor, 5,625-page delayed writes, failed invalidation, PTE mismatch and recycle; `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed the protected-buffer/fence/reservation-to-accessor takeover and an ambiguous-write retention case. `git diff --check` passed. The scratch page must remain retained if rollback left entries referring to it, and throughout any uncertain operation. Dell generation 188 partial and generation 187 full fallback are unchanged; no physical mapping or display write occurred. Next deliver a real ownership and cross-boot strategy and a bounded flip/completion implementation instead of treating these host transactions as a hardware desktop.

**Multi-page GGTT MMIO accessor (local, host simulation only):** Added unwired `intel_bdw_ggtt_extent_mmio.h` for a lease spanning audited UC-mapped PTE pages. **Protected scanout buffer linked to GGTT extent policy (local, host simulation only):** Added unwired `intel_bdw_scanout_mapping.h`, which obtains the adopted protected buffer's exact immutable DMA page array, holds a buffer reference and token-bound scanout-mapping gate, reserves a matching GGTT extent, and passes those facts through a checked adapter to the large-range transaction. A successful flip cannot release the old buffer for GPU use until its GGTT mapping has been retired; a failed or uncertain write/invalidation keeps the buffer, gate and reservation. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed real protected buffer/fence handoff plus a fake two-page GGTT mapping, rejection while still scanned out, flip then unmap/reuse, and a fork-isolated failed write/invalidation retaining all resources. No Dell boot or recovery path changed; generation 185 partial and generation 184 full rollback remain.

**Multi-page GGTT transaction policy (local, host simulation only):** Added unwired `intel_bdw_ggtt_extent_bind.h` for a pinned, immutable DMA-page list and an exact large reservation. It validates bounds and backend ownership/quiescence, checks every original PTE is invalid before writing, drains and verifies writes, and requires quiescence, exact PTEs, invalidation and readback before retirement. A possibly delivered failed write is drained before rollback; failed drain, unexpected PTE, lost ownership or failed retirement quarantines the entire lease and its pages. Host `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_bind` passed a 5,625-page delayed-write simulation, failure on entry 513, failed invalidation, modified PTE, wrong backend, non-quiescence and invalid DMA; `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_space` and `git diff --check` passed. This header is not in the built kernel or called by production; the fake backend supplies all ownership, non-aliasing, DMA and quiescence assertions. It accepts only initially invalid PTEs and cannot take over firmware scratch mappings, which may be present on the Dell. It does not pin buffers, install GGTT entries, control the display, prove ordering on hardware or handle cross-boot retention. Next bind this policy to actual retained protected buffers and a safe, serialized multi-page MMIO backend; independently establish firmware/display ownership and a cross-boot retirement path before any hardware write. Dell generation 185 partial and generation 184 full rollback remain unchanged.

**Scanout-sized GGTT software reservations (local, not wired):** The existing allocator limits `reserve()` to 32 pages inside one PTE page; a 3200×1800×4 buffer requires 5,625 pages. Added a separate `reserveExtent()` for aligned ranges up to 65,536 pages, sharing the existing bitmap/token registry and preserving all restrictions on old small reservations. Host `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_space` passed two nonoverlapping 5,625-page aligned extents, competition with small reservations, invalid sizes/alignment and stale-token reuse; `test_intel_bdw_ggtt_bind` passed unchanged. This only reserves software address slots: the existing binder still admits at most 32 pages in one PTE page, and no hardware PTE checks, ownership, mapping, invalidation or display takeover are supplied. It is not used by the desktop, paired, recovery-gated or deployed. Next design and test a bounded multi-PTE-page mapping transaction that retains all pages/reservations through partial failure and has a verified retirement path; only then consider any hardware access. Dell generation 185 partial, generation 184 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Intel protected-output transfer to scanout lifetime (local, not wired):** Added `intel_bdw_scanout_lifetime.h`, an unwired adapter that transfers a completed, taken handoff's existing protected buffer reference and exclusive gate into the device-neutral active/pending policy without releasing either. Adoption rejects untaken, wrong-display, CPU-mappable, still-used or unreserved buffers. Previous scanout is returned for GPU reuse only after a caller-supplied matching flip proof; a failed release retains the reference and blocks new adoption. Display quiescence is a separate caller-supplied proof and does not prove engine retirement. `BdwGpuBufferHandoffCompleted` distinguishes the completed reservation from the fresh reservation: the first host run caught that difference before the fix. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passes real handoff/fence transfer, owner detach and handle close while active, wrong live/display rejection, replacement, and a fork-isolated sticky failure retaining its reference. Guarded kernel built/relinked SHA-256 `b466ce1fce9a0f20284a3d2760c147bad10d01dfdc0e2613eb0b2c70f79803e3`; `git diff --check` passed. The adapter is not called by production and does not establish a GGTT mapping, display ownership, cache visibility, vblank/flip completion, stale-producer exclusion or hardware reset safety. No physical change; generation 185 partial, generation 184 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain. Next establish an identity-bound safe Broadwell scanout mapping and hardware completion mechanism before wiring the adapter to display writes.

**Direct scanout lifetime groundwork (local, not wired):** On current generation 185 boot `891042c310504a2b8e56cc6d9f8704fc`, read-only `bridge hardware gpu-display-state` reported pipe A primary control `0x98000000`, stride 12800, surface/live 0; other sampled pipes read zero. Added `compositor_scanout_lifetime.h`, an unwired device-neutral state policy retaining active and pending identities across renderer loss and uncertain updates. It refuses a second pending update or incomplete producer, returns the old active buffer only after a caller-supplied matching flip-completion proof, and returns both retained buffers only after a caller-supplied display-quiescence proof. The policy neither pins actual buffers nor proves rendering completion, flip completion, vblank, firmware ownership or reset safety; no Intel register is written and no device behavior changed. Linux's [KMS documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/gpu/drm-kms.html) describes waiting for rendering and retaining old buffers until completion. Next integrate with actual OS-owned buffer references and design Broadwell-specific safe display takeover and completion evidence before attempting any physical plane writes. Current generation 185 partial, generation 184 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain.

**Independent GPU submissions can pass blocked dependencies (local, not deployed):** The single Intel worker previously stalled every client behind the oldest pending dependency. Queue admission now chooses the oldest ready request that can be proved independent of every earlier queued request: nonzero distinct owner incarnations, distinct retained contexts, and no shared retained `BdwGpuBuffer`. Unknown identity/context, shared context/buffer, same owner, or more than 4096 pairwise object comparisons preserves original order. Current Intel PRIME imports retain the same buffer object and independent allocations own distinct pages; any future importer that creates different wrappers for one backing must update this proof. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed independent-client progress, same-owner/shared-context/shared-buffer/unknown refusal, a three-request transitive shared-buffer case, and existing cancellation/queue tests. Guarded kernel built/relinked SHA-256 `647ef99ea95ab4ba5941bdd4499b5d5245d186de2e44786e6c5f16f9a67452b8`; `git diff --check` passed. This is not yet QEMU-gated or physically deployed and does not resolve an active GPU hang, stalled renderer exit, or untracked cross-device memory sharing. Current Dell generation 166 partial with automatic blocked recovery and generation 165 full-frame rollback remain unchanged. Next validate independence and preserved ordering using a two-client physical fixture with one synthetic blocked dependency, then run real GL/Vulkan coexistence before deployment.

**Constrain application GPU worker to identified owners (local, not deployed):** The application submission worker is now initialized in known-owner-only mode: pre-submission registration and ordinary submissions reject owner zero, and handoff submissions must match the nonzero session owner. The ordinary user ioctl captures the current leader incarnation before entering this worker; separate kernel-authored probe workers retain their previous mode. Consequently, on a newly booted kernel using this mode there cannot be unknown-origin application work waiting to be blocked by a stalled owner's freeze, and a different identified client remains admissible. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed unknown-origin and mismatched-handoff rejection, another-owner progress while frozen, and the integrated actual exec-ioctl cancellation path using known-owner mode. Guarded kernel built/relinked SHA-256 `499d688ece9509e41b0b2adbcaaffc86c225ce219ceb11e69337785ac8d4c683`. This limits collateral queue impact; it does not release a stalled owner's handoff/session, ensure a replacement compositor starts, bound its exit, or prove no other GPU path can affect it. No QEMU gate or Dell deployment occurred. Current generation 164 partial, generation 163 full-frame rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Drain all never-started submissions from frozen renderer (local, not deployed):** Cancelling only the blocked handoff could leave other submissions from the same renderer at the head of the GPU queue. Once the handoff is cancelled and its owner frozen, the service now cancels that incarnation's other queued requests under the queue lock, signals their fences as failed, tracks their snapshot releases, and retires any associated protected handoff slots only after each never-started snapshot is released. Active/quarantined and foreign-owner work is not cancelled; failure remains conservative. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed a session with blocked and ready same-owner requests, two protected outputs, and foreign queued work that still executes; a separate case confirmed active work survives the drain. Guarded non-test kernel built/relinked SHA-256 `67e4d8565af96e98a9a71f2de8f0aef0ede4327ade5779d0814a306aa0618582`; `git diff --check` passed. This postdates the Dell renderer test below and has not been QEMU-gated or physically deployed. It improves queue progress but does not bound a frozen owner whose exit stalls, nor prove a real GPU hang/reset. No integrated process/driver or physical fault fixture has run. **Recovery freeze owned by the handoff session (local, not exposed or deployed):** Added session operations to begin owner-bound blocked cancellation/freeze, inspect outstanding work, abandon recovery, and retire the freeze when the owner is destroyed. The session also records a freeze if cancellation succeeded but its later slot release returned an invariant error, so cleanup can still thaw it. No QEMU gate or Dell deployment occurred; generation 155 partial, generation 154 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Never-submitted cancelled outputs can retire (local, not deployed):** A confirmed blocked cancellation previously left the protected output slot quarantined forever even though the queue proved the exact request never entered the GPU. After the queue atomically cancels that request, signals failure and releases its snapshot, the handoff adapter now retires the slot and its buffer gate. If gate release fails, it restores quarantine and reports failure; a generic failed fence or active/uncertain request still cannot use this path. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed four consecutive cancelled submissions using the same output, stale-ticket replacement, cancel-versus-admission races, ready/active refusal, and an injected gate-token invariant failure which remains quarantined. The renderer still retains its Vulkan context and parks after this cancellation; do not infer automatic process restart, safe global GPU drain or physical validation. No QEMU gate or Dell deployment occurred; generation 155 partial, generation 154 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Intel ioctl fatal-exit lifetime and shared-buffer audit (local, not deployed):** The new exec preparation registration uses a node on the calling thread's kernel stack. `IntelRenderIoctl` now uses the scheduler's existing `KernelOperationGuard` for its entire operation so a fatal exit is deferred until preparation, snapshot and other ioctl state have unwound; the handoff-control syscall already had this guard. Existing interruptible waits check `terminalPending`. Source audit shows the scheduler delays leader reaping for live thread-group peers, and GPU snapshots separately retain buffers and contexts across file close. Added a host regression with two GPU files sharing a buffer: close the renderer file while its work and a foreign owner's work are queued, prove its context and buffer remain retained, then show renderer-owner work can reach zero while the foreign work still uses the same buffer. `test_intel_bdw_buffer` and scheduler lifecycle fixture in `test_vfs_paths` passed; the latter tests deferred terminal publication generally, not an integrated fatal Intel ioctl. This is not proof of complete process teardown or permission to reclaim shared storage based on owner counts. Automatic restart remains unwired; no QEMU gate or Dell deployment occurred. Generation 155 partial, generation 154 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Exec preparation tracking (local, not deployed):** The normal experimental Intel render and store-probe exec ioctls now register their leader incarnation with the submission service before taking the timeline lock or copying an exec request, and unregister only after fence publication or failed-snapshot cleanup. The same queue mutex serializes this registration with owner freeze: existing same-owner preparation is counted, existing unknown-origin preparation contributes to `unknown`, and new same/unknown-owner preparation is refused while frozen. Other identified owners remain allowed. This does not account for kernel-side direct submission producers before admission or prove safety of shared files, foreign GPU uses, process teardown or cancellation of a stuck preparation. **Retirement accounting and cancellation/admission race (local, not deployed):** An owner work inspection could previously report zero after a completed/cancelled snapshot was removed from the queue but before its retained references were released outside the queue lock. The submission service now registers each such release under the queue lock and counts it as `retiring` for its incarnation, or as `unknown` for an untagged snapshot, until release completes. A release/invariant failure invalidates subsequent inspections rather than reporting a false drain. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed explicit overlapping retirement-ledger accounting and 32 isolated races of combined blocked cancellation/freeze against a new submission: that submission was either counted in the frozen queue or refused. The ledger unit test does not force an actual snapshot release to pause, and the freeze still does not track snapshots being prepared in an ioctl before queue admission, shared-file/foreign-owner uses, other GPU paths, or the full process lifetime. These remain necessary before automatic teardown/restart. No QEMU gate or physical deployment occurred; generation 155 partial, generation 154 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged.

**Atomic blocked cancellation and owner freeze (local, not wired or deployed):** Added a combined submission-service operation which checks the handoff owner and submitting incarnation, cancels only its still-blocked queued request, and freezes that incarnation under the same queue lock. **Atomic owner admission freeze (local, not wired or deployed):** The Intel submission service can now freeze one nonzero owner incarnation and inspect its queued/active/quarantined work under the same mutex used for admission. While frozen it rejects that owner's submissions and all unknown-owner submissions; a different identified owner may still submit. Only the matching incarnation can thaw. Both ordinary and handoff submission paths honor the freeze, and handoff rejection happens before arming its output. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed other-owner/unknown handling, handoff rejection and a 32-iteration concurrent freeze-versus-submit race in which either the submission was included in the frozen snapshot or it was rejected. **GPU submission owner identity (local, not deployed):** Intel ioctl snapshots now carry the submitter's non-reused leader incarnation in addition to their diagnostic PID and context; kernel-created/untracked snapshots have owner zero. A queue-locked inspection reports queued, active and quarantined work for one incarnation and separately counts outstanding unknown-owner work. It is deliberately only a snapshot: without an admission freeze, a new submission may race immediately afterward, so it is not permission to tear down a renderer. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed same-PID/different-incarnation separation, unknown-owner reporting and queued-to-active-to-complete transitions, along with the cancellation tests below. The guarded kernel built with symbol relink, SHA-256 `7c445d19cdd290e4f92801a48ab451b4185ca2e7e581b209b7b8b66370a19115`. **Queued cancellation/admission race:** Extended `test_intel_bdw_buffer` with 32 isolated concurrent races between signaling the blocked dependency and cancelling its owner-bound handoff. It passed with a real host mutex: either cancellation retired the still-queued snapshot and failed its fence without admission, or the now-ready snapshot was admitted and cancellation refused it. The test also checks the cancelled output remains quarantined and successful active work finishes normally. This is host concurrency evidence, not a physical Intel or complete renderer-restart test. Source inspection shows execution snapshots retain referenced GPU buffers and contexts, but the current handoff queue uses an internal shared owner rather than a per-process incarnation, so a single cancelled ticket does not prove every GPU use by the renderer has retired. Do not destroy the parked Vulkan process solely on cancellation until that whole-owner lifetime can be established. **Blocked compositor submission cancellation (local, not deployed):** Added owner/ticket-bound handoff op `BROOK_GPU_HANDOFF_CANCEL_BLOCKED`: under the existing offscreen-to-queue lock order it cancels only the exact request while still queued and with an unresolved dependency. Worker admission and cancellation are serialized, so active, already-ready, wrong-owner and stale requests cannot be cancelled by this operation. Cancellation retires the never-submitted snapshot and signals its completion fences as failed; the handoff output is conservatively quarantined rather than reused. If failure signaling itself violates an invariant after retirement, the queue now quarantines the entry and poisons itself rather than leaving an invalid snapshot runnable. After 30 seconds of an uncertain fence the desktop renderer attempts this operation only for a pending ticket, records the result, and continues retaining its context; older kernels simply reject the new op. This can unblock unrelated later GPU jobs but does not yet restart that renderer or recover its quarantined output. Host `test_intel_bdw_buffer` passed pending cancellation, wrong owner, ready/active refusal, subsequent queue progress, quarantine and signaling-invariant failure; compositor package `/nix/store/3q8x3593yx995aiwp1c7m5d5pjpnqa97-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1` built with fence-policy/supervisor/damage/tile checks. Guarded kernel built with symbol relink, SHA-256 `b03cf4462928f5bbb3c3f93f4caa4e8bc7b7d5b49d60f460850712581c1a7155`. Neither kernel nor renderer has been packaged for boot, QEMU-gated or tested on the Dell; current generation 155 partial and generation 154 full rollback remain unchanged. Next construct an integrated blocked-dependency fixture that independently proves cancellation cannot race active admission, and assess safe renderer restart before physical deployment.

**Persistent fence diagnostics and remaining recovery gap:** Added local renderer logging after 30 seconds of an unresolved handoff and at most once per minute thereafter, including the kernel handoff observation and errno; resources remain retained. A possible next step is identity-bound cancellation of an explicitly abandoned queued compositor submission under the queue lock, but the queue/ticket/fence lifecycle must distinguish a provably never-submitted cancellation from active or quarantined work before releasing anything; arbitrary unsignaled dependencies must not cause a system-wide reboot. **Late Vulkan-fence recovery (local renderer, physical fixture):** A renderer no longer has to park forever solely because `vkWaitForFences` returned `VK_TIMEOUT`: it retains all resources, polls the owner-bound kernel handoff ticket, and only when that reports successful completion asks the Vulkan renderer to retire. Retirement is permitted only for a timeout and only after `vkGetFenceStatus` returns success; it destroys the now-safe renderer, releases the ticket, resets the render context and retries from a full frame. Submit errors, device loss, failed/unknown handoff fences and indefinitely pending work remain quarantined; no speculative resource release or reset was added. `brook-vulkan-timeout-test` issued a real zero-timeout fence wait, verified that an uncertain renderer could not be ordinarily destroyed, waited for its Vulkan fence to retire, created a new renderer and checked every output pixel. It passed on host llvmpipe and on Intel HD 5500 on Dell boot `89fced48f0824e698ebc3e80f69cd95f`, job `0e2e51e253f24017951657544ce3c658`, exit 0 and descendants drained, transfer `build/hardware/dell-late-fence-fixture-20261111/receipt.json`, package `/nix/store/j5m799mnqa17awl21pcl7h3sv3vp3bcp-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1`. The fixture retains resources indefinitely if the fence never becomes safe. It tests the Vulkan renderer's fence/retirement path, not the full desktop's dual-fence/ticket recovery or an actual GPU hang. The updated desktop renderer and boot console logging below have not been packaged or deployed; current generation 152 partial, generation 151 full rollback and SSD/USB recovery remain unchanged. Next exercise the desktop dual-fence recovery via a bounded fault fixture before deployment.

**Boot renderer failure diagnostics prepared locally:** The GPU worker already escalates an unsafe engine stop to kernel panic recovery, and the renderer deliberately parks if Vulkan completion or retained-resource destruction is uncertain; changing that lifetime rule without a proven reset remains unsafe. The boot startup entry now uses `run --console`, making supervisor restarts and renderer errors visible in the normal kernel console/debug log. To avoid a console-update/render feedback loop, unbounded `--watch` mode no longer emits periodic successful-frame lines unless `BROOK_RENDER_PROGRESS` is explicitly set; bounded `--frames` output and error/retry reporting remain. The exact startup verifier covers the new entry and preparation rejects both old and new duplicate entries. Preparation/verifier host suites passed (9 and 7 tests); package `/nix/store/jsmyji81sy9s4pq9p9699p134jjvnx6n-brook-vulkan-compositor-0.1` built with supervisor, damage and tile tests. **Internal region-copy lease guard:** `CompositorPresentProbe` has an internal-only region mode which requires a still-active lease owned by the same renderer, a previously complete leased scanout, matching display/backdrop generations and no pending repair. The OS still holds its scanout mapping lock over the operation; this does not make multiple region updates atomic with each other or guarantee tear-free physical scanout. Before connecting it, bind the retained base to the non-reused window/backing identities and a complete scene, prove damage covers all changes, and design bounded multi-region publication with failure/fallback semantics. **Submission timing diagnostic built locally:** Added compile-time opt-in `BROOK_GPU_SUBMISSION_TIMING` (default off). **Submission latency investigation:** Source inspection of the currently deployed worker identifies a concrete candidate for the 112–117 ms submit-to-fence time. Every submitted snapshot reconstructs the GPU execution tables, republishes private execution pages and calls `BdwExecSnapshotSyncForDevice`, which CLFLUSHes every page of every referenced buffer. After a safely stopped submission, queue retirement calls `BdwExecSnapshotSyncForCpu`, which repeats that full-buffer cache operation before signaling completion. The recurring full-resolution renderer supplies multiple 3200×1800 buffers, so these operations can cover many tens of MiB per submission; the worker also resets and re-prepares the engine on each job. This is a source-based hypothesis, not a measurement or evidence that the flushes are unnecessary. Do not skip cache maintenance or change the reset policy without proving CPU/GPU visibility, ownership and failure recovery. Next add bounded, opt-in measurements around preparation/cache publication, device execution/reset and post-completion cache synchronization on a guarded candidate; compare those on Dell against a small-buffer control, and retain the existing recovery fixture and fallback. No new kernel or physical experiment was deployed in this investigation.

**Intel output GPU admission gate (local, not wired):** `BdwGpuBuffer` now offers an opt-in kernel-token handoff reservation that excludes ordinary GPU reservations and CPU-domain transitions, permits only one matching handoff GPU use, and remains held after that use retires until explicitly released. `BdwExecSnapshotBindHandoff` binds the reserved output to an exact writable snapshot and its pending signal fence; normal snapshot reservation then uses the matching gate. Host tests passed competing submissions, wrong tokens/fences, concurrent ordinary-use attempts, retirement while the gate remains held, and a partial snapshot-reservation failure that consumes the token and requires discarding the snapshot before a fresh token. The guarded kernel builds; this opt-in route is not connected to the live handoff adapter or deployed. It does not revoke existing or future writable CPU mappings, establish OS-owned scanout, prove cache/device retirement, or prevent a trusted kernel caller from mismanaging tokens. Address mapping ownership and integrate with the retained handoff and authoritative scene/display generations before use.

**Handoff buffer/fence admission relationship (local, not wired):** `BdwExecSnapshotWritesWithSignal` checks that the exact retained output buffer is writable in the same prepared/reserved Intel submission snapshot as the exact pending signal fence. `BdwHandoffArm` now requires that evidence before marking a retained output in flight; its callers must serialize snapshot admission/release and prevent later writes. Host Intel-buffer tests use real snapshot, buffer and fence objects to reject an unrelated fence and a read-only object, then test owner death before retirement and during OS presentation; both Intel-buffer and generic handoff CTests passed. The guarded kernel also built. This relationship proves neither that GPU commands actually write the buffer nor that a malicious/subsequent submission cannot modify it; the adapter remains unconnected to the real compositor, process cleanup or display and has not been physically deployed. Next establish exclusive output ownership and authoritative desktop scene/display generations, then wire the resource/fence transition and publication under the appropriate locks.

**GPU-owned compositor output works offscreen on Intel:** The multi-source Vulkan renderer now has an optional separate DMA-BUF destination (`brook_vk_renderer_create_multi_output` / `brook_vk_renderer_compose_multi_output`). It checks descriptor limits and stable identities, rejects source/destination aliases, waits for source sync-files, acquires/releases external ownership for all buffers and quarantines source/destination resources after uncertain completion. On Dell boot `80edc725a7c64822a8f1bf9f5886b1c8`, job `da383566747a4e6eace1a46d630dfef9` rendered three two-source scenes into a distinct Intel GEM buffer; both producer fences were initially pending in each round, and after GPU completion the test independently switched the destination to CPU access and matched every pixel. Same-fd and duplicated source/destination alias rejections passed. Job `0769ba5a5f9f4cfaa811a1b56715d9e1` passed the existing multi-source CPU-output path; llvmpipe renderer/surface regressions and the Nix build passed. The test-only CPU readback proves pixels; the output API itself performs no CPU pixel readback. It still waits synchronously for completion, requires the caller to ensure the destination is free before writing, and has no OS-owned display, scene capture, process-failure cleanup or scanout integration. Preserve all resources on UNCERTAIN and use the existing CPU desktop until the missing handoff is proven.

**Intel handoff resource adapter (host-tested, not wired):** `src/kernel/src/intel_bdw_handoff.h` binds the two-slot policy to real `BdwGpuBuffer` and `BdwFence` references. It retains the buffer at reservation, retains the trusted submission fence before GPU access, keeps both through uncertain owner exit, observes actual fence status, and retains a completed buffer through OS presentation. The existing `test_intel_bdw_buffer` uses actual buffer/fence reference code to check owner death while pending and owner death during presentation; it and `test_compositor_handoff` passed host CTest. It is not yet called by the kernel compositor or a process-exit path, does not establish that the supplied fence belongs to the submitted GPU job, does not allocate or display the output, and does not create an authoritative whole-desktop scene epoch. The integrating caller must use a sleepable mutex, respect lock ordering, supply an authenticated submission/fence binding before exposing GPU access, and retain uncertain work until completion or verified device reset. Continue to a real API and VM failure/resize tests before physical use.

**Display handoff policy (host-only, not wired):** Added `src/kernel/src/compositor_handoff.h` and `test_compositor_handoff`. The two-slot policy distinguishes reserved, submitted, ready, OS-presenting and quarantined output; binds an owner incarnation and non-reused ticket; rejects stale scene/display generations; retains uncertain GPU work across owner death; and does not free a slot while the OS is presenting it. Host CTest passed. Callers must mark in-flight before GPU access and serialize the take against authoritative scene/display generations; the policy does not itself pin memory, inspect a fence, stop the existing kernel compositor, allocate scanout, publish output, or prove recovery after a real process/GPU failure. **Firmware MTRR baseline (QEMU):** Boot protocol v5 captures a double-sampled fingerprint of Intel boot-CPU MTRR capability, default, variable/fixed registers and physical-address width before replacing firmware page tables. Host tests cover changed/invalid MTRR fingerprints. This is a compact diagnostic fingerprint and current-CPU check, not assurance of other CPUs, unrecorded aliases or firmware resource coordination; only Intel is currently admitted. No Dell deployment or physical S5 test has occurred.

**UEFI memory-attribute correction:** UEFI `GetMemoryMap()` attributes are capabilities, not necessarily current protection or cache settings (`https://uefi.org/specs/UEFI/2.10/07_Services_Boot_Services.html`). The runtime map check incorrectly treated EFI_MEMORY_RO capability as permission to accept read-only runtime data; it now requires runtime-data mappings writable regardless of that bit. Host boot-resource and alias tests pass, including the capability case. This is local and does not establish firmware cache-type compatibility: compare actual firmware mappings and CPU cache state rather than inferring current settings from descriptor capabilities before enabling physical calls.

**Ian's USB-specific recovery suggestion:** Prefer investigating a USB-controller/adapter health trigger for the opt-in boot recovery instead of treating general gateway unreachability as a USB fault. None alone proves the reported whole-stack lockup will set a detectable bit, and a disconnected adapter, network outage, controller fault and stalled transfer must remain distinguishable. **Local queue failure propagation:** A failed active request now marks its reserved or armed buffers failed before use counts can drop. When the engine stop is uncertain, the ledger quarantines the active snapshot, poisons the engine queue and marks queued requests failed so their GEM waits report EIO; queued snapshots remain reapable and releasable, while the uncertain active snapshot cannot be reaped. Host tests use different active and queued buffers to verify both waits report EIO and the quarantined job cannot be reaped; the guarded kernel builds. This is an unwired ledger, with no live worker, completion wakeup or application EXECBUFFER2 support. The physical Dell is unchanged.

**Local queued GEM wait accounting:** Enqueue into the ownership ledger now reserves GPU-use counts before publishing a queued snapshot, so GEM_WAIT does not report idle while an admitted job waits for its worker. Preparation accepts the reserved state; arming transfers that reservation without incrementing again, and cancellation can release an unsubmitted reservation without a hardware reset. Tests use real GEM snapshots to cover queue capacity, duplicate insertion, queued zero-timeout wait, cancellation, arming, retirement and reference counts; the guarded kernel builds. The queue remains an unwired ledger with external serialization, not a worker or public EXECBUFFER2 implementation. Next prepare and verify a new candidate before staging, inspect its admission stage, and run the one-shot only if the preflight permits it. The clear operation compares the full exact owned PTE set, clears it after reset, invalidates and reads back, quarantining on ambiguity; host tests cover mismatch, failed writes/invalidation and non-idle refusal. This does not solve unexpected panic/reset before cleanup or firmware activity across boots.

**GEM wait deployed; HasVK reaches execbuf2 check:** The Dell now runs `dell-gem-wait-20261106`, generation 65 slot 0, retaining generation 64 slot 1 (`build/hardware/dell-gem-wait-activate-20261106/receipt.json`); boot `3be272a1963946df943fa81b0fedde03`, session `b10e0cb35fd0475295756afe297ee888`. The candidate passed the guarded QEMU panic/reset/USB fixture (`build/hardware/guard-gem-wait-qemu-20261106/`). GEM_WAIT uses retained buffer references, GPU-use counts, monotonic deadlines and 1 ms interruptible polling, with ETIME, EINTR and sticky EIO handling; the future submission owner must account uses before publication and mark failed/uncertain snapshots. Host tests cover idle, timeout, completion, interruption, invalid handles/flags and error state. The Dell `/boot/IGEMPROB` passed idle wait and error argument checks (`gem-probe-job.json`); busy/timeouts have only host coverage, since public submission is still disabled. Forced HasVK `vulkaninfo --summary` now passes its GEM wait check and fails on missing execbuf2 (`vulkaninfo-hasvk-job.json`), so no Vulkan device or rendering exists yet. Desktop is ready. The local affinity change is included in this candidate, but no GPU worker uses it yet.

**Local GEM GPU-use accounting:** A retained snapshot now increments an atomic use count on each buffer when armed and drops those counts only when released with a proven safe stop. Host tests cover armed counts, refusal to release uncertain work, overlapping uses and underflow refusal; the guarded kernel builds. This is not yet a wait implementation: there are no waiters, timeout accounting or wakeups, and the submission owner must publish counts before exposing work. The change is not deployed. Do not advertise `I915_PARAM_HAS_WAIT_TIMEOUT` until GEM_WAIT handles in-flight work and failures correctly.

**HasVK now reaches the i915 node:** On generation 64, staged `vulkaninfo --summary` forced to the installed Intel HasVK ICD reaches the driver and exits with `kernel missing gem wait (VK_ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED)` (`build/hardware/dell-rcs-gem-probe-activate-20261106/vulkaninfo-hasvk-job.json`). A first launch omitted staged libffi and failed in the dynamic loader before the successful diagnostic invocation. Implement real GEM wait/in-flight tracking, wakeups, timeouts and reset/error handling before advertising the wait capability; an unconditional idle result would become unsafe as soon as application execution is enabled.

**Local kernel-thread affinity:** The scheduler's shared eligibility check now honors explicit `cpuAffinity` for kernel threads as well as user tasks; the default `-1` remains unrestricted and the idle task remains eligible. Normal, priority-inheritance and stall pick paths all call that shared check. Host scheduler tests pass, and both the guarded kernel and the opt-in first-dispatch build compile. The later eight-CPU fixture passed with AP3 relying on production affinity instead of the prior test-only reservation; see the current SMP result above. Building that fixture exposed five missing GPU callbacks in standalone memory-test ELFs; fail-closed test-only stubs restore the full build. The change is not deployed to the Dell and does not solve the GPU runner's long-held page-table lock.

**Local render request ownership ledger:** `intel_bdw_exec_queue.h` adds a bounded externally locked FIFO for retained GEM snapshots: one active request, owner-scoped observation/reaping, queued cancellation, no duplicate snapshot ownership, and permanent quarantine plus queue poisoning after an uncertain stop. The host buffer test exercises real snapshots, owner isolation, cancellation, capacity and uncertain execution. It is not connected to an ioctl or worker and has not been deployed. The present hardware runner holds `g_kernelPtLock` with interrupts disabled while waiting and its DMA admission requires the BSP; `ProcessCanRunOnCpu` currently exempts all kernel threads from CPU affinity. An application worker therefore needs a real solution to both constraints, not just setting `cpuAffinity`. Linux's [Gen8 batch dispatch](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/uml/linux/+/7308e92756d5891d58e7bcae01a516514583921d/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/gen8_engine_cs.c) uses bit 8 for PPGTT/non-secure dispatch, but that is not proof Brook has implemented the rest of hardware isolation and command validation.

**Physical GEM-backed command and data passed:** The Dell runs `dell-rcs-gem-probe-20261106`, generation 64 slot 1, retaining generation 63 slot 0 (`build/hardware/dell-rcs-gem-probe-activate-20261106/receipt.json`); boot `57d3032b082746eb96b7b4f2de1a70fe`, session `35d9d1a5413240abbcdf02f31b5fb50b`. Engine reset and PAT restoration passed, forcewake was released, IPEIR was zero and desktop remained ready (`build/hardware/dell-rcs-gem-probe-activate-20261106/gpu-result.json`). The bridge does not report the raw nonce. The objects intentionally remain retained through this boot; do not repeat the one-shot. This is a fixed private command, not arbitrary application submission, a draw or 3D acceleration. Command isolation, scheduling, synchronization and reset-safe reclamation are still required.

**Local GEM snapshot attached to private RCS object:** `BdwRenderOneShot::AttachSnapshot` now builds its own PPGTT pages and ring from a caller-retained GEM snapshot. Execution refuses an attached snapshot unless its image has been published and `ArmSnapshot` succeeds with the snapshot's existing DMA/cache/PPGTT proofs. A snapshot detached before arming permanently disables that one-shot, preventing a stale ring from being submitted; republishing after arming is refused. Host tests attach real GEM buffers, inspect the ring and PTEs, and exercise publish failure, refusal to arm without proofs, detachment and cleanup. The guarded kernel builds. The attachment path is not yet connected to the physical private test or public ioctls. The future owner must retain the snapshot across uncertain execution and provide command isolation and synchronization; this does not authorize GPU submission.

**Local snapshot-to-render image integration:** `BdwExecSnapshotBuildRenderImage` uses one retained GEM snapshot to construct both its PPGTT and the RCS ring pointing at its batch. It rejects a ring overlapping page tables or mapping workspace, revokes the prepared-image proof on a failed rebuild, and still requires the caller to establish all ownership, command safety, DMA/cache and reset guarantees. Host tests use actual retained buffer objects to check writable/read-only PTEs, batch address, ring encoding, alias rejection and failed-rebuild arm refusal. The guarded kernel builds. This helper is not connected to the live device, and no application work has been submitted.

**Physical PPGTT data write passed:** The Dell now runs `dell-rcs-ppgtt-store-20261106`, generation 63 slot 0, retaining generation 62 slot 1 (`build/hardware/dell-rcs-ppgtt-store-activate-20261106/receipt.json`); boot `0ebbbfcd85e14e37885dd365e8a0d1b6`, session `e175e477e771482c9743fcf891f07dd0`. **Physical PPGTT batch fetch passed:** The Dell now runs `dell-rcs-ppgtt-probe-20261106`, generation 62 slot 1, with generation 61 retained in slot 0 (`build/hardware/dell-rcs-ppgtt-probe-activate-20261106/receipt.json`); boot `e1c46b79f2e742858e4405bdb6eea6de`, session `8b49b003d11b48b8995a32a307261b63`. **Local RCS ring builder:** `intel_bdw_render_ring.h` factors the 56-dword ring used by the tested private render run and can encode a 48-bit PPGTT batch address for a future application submission. The previous GGTT sequence remains covered by the existing one-shot test; new host tests check both address modes, bounds, alignment and completion marker. The guarded kernel builds. The PPGTT variant has not been run on hardware and selecting a per-process address space does not prove command privilege or isolation. Linux's [i915 command definitions](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gpu_commands.h) identify the bit used for PPGTT selection; command privilege handling and the full submission lifecycle require separate validation. Nothing has been deployed.

**Local EXECBUFFER2 decoding groundwork:** `BdwIntelCopyExecSnapshot` copies the x86-64 i915 request and object array once into kernel memory, checks pointer overflow and rejects unsupported contexts, engines, relocations, fences, reserved fields and unpinned objects. It then resolves the file's handles into the existing retained-buffer snapshot. It is internal and is not wired to an ioctl or a GPU submission path; successful decoding neither validates GPU commands nor permits DMA. Focused host tests cover successful snapshot creation, rejected flags and fields, pointer overflow and first/second usercopy faults; struct sizes and offsets were checked against installed libdrm headers. The guarded kernel builds. This work is not deployed; actual scheduling, command isolation, synchronization and reset-safe cleanup remain necessary.

**Local i915 identity queries:** `intel_bdw_ioctl.cpp` now handles x86-64 `I915_GETPARAM` for the admitted Dell device and revision and reports zero for several unsupported execution capabilities; unknown parameters return `EINVAL`. The host ioctl test covers identity, absent execution, unknown selector and failed usercopy; the guarded kernel builds. `scripts/workloads/intel_gem_probe.c` now checks these through real ioctls, including invalid pointers, but this kernel and updated probe have **not** been deployed or tested on the Dell. The running generation 61 still returns `ENOTTY` for GETPARAM. Do not advertise execution until a real scheduler, security, synchronization and reset-safe lifetime are in place.

**Opt-in Intel render-node candidate:** `/dev/dri/renderD129` and `/sys/dev/char/226:129/device/*` are now published only with `/etc/dell-gpu-intel-user-test`, armed recovery and exact live Dell PCI/D0 admission. **Intel ioctl usercopy tests:** The basic Intel ioctl dispatcher is now `intel_bdw_ioctl.cpp`, used by the kernel syscall adapter with explicit user-copy callbacks. Host tests exercise version strings, inaccessible input/output, failed GEM-create copyout with handle/backing rollback, rounded GEM creation, WB mmap-offset and unsupported WC mode, close and mapping lifetime. The guarded kernel and focused host tests pass. This tests the actual ioctl dispatcher but not the kernel's complete mmap, fd publication, dup/fork or SCM path. No Intel open/sysfs node is published and there is no execution backend exposed yet; no Dell deployment occurred.

**Internal Intel fd/ioctl/mmap plumbing:** A distinct `DevIntelDri` fd type now participates in refcounting, close, fstat and SCM_RIGHTS; its mmap path retains the Intel buffer backing and maps the requested page range from chunked kernel allocations. Internal ioctl handling recognizes DRM version/capability, GEM create/close and write-back mmap-offset; unsupported caching modes and submission remain rejected. Failed GEM-create copyout closes the newly allocated handle. No open path or sysfs node publishes this type yet, so these syscalls cannot be reached from userspace and do not advertise a functional device. Guarded kernel builds; buffer/mapping and PPGTT host tests pass. The generic fd-table stress test also passed in an isolated build with `-Wno-error=class-memaccess` for a pre-existing `pipe.h` warning. The new syscall path itself still needs direct usercopy/mmap/dup/fork/SCM tests before publication; execution, synchronization, i915 capability/query/context ioctls and actual scheduling remain incomplete. No Dell deployment occurred.

**Application-buffer DMA and CPU-cache preparation:** `BdwExecSnapshotInspectDma` now takes a point-in-time Dell VT-d observation before/after checking each retained buffer's current kernel mapping, physical range, reserved-memory exclusion and PMM Device/Kernel ownership. Unlike private one-shot pages, application pages may legitimately have user mapping references. It is BSP/reset-armed only and does not authorize DMA or exclude later IOMMU changes. Buffer cache synchronization uses CLFLUSH in 16-page groups with migration/interrupt exclusion per group; the caller must exclude concurrent CPU access and separately flush device caches. Snapshot arming now requires successful PPGTT construction, buffer CPU sync, DMA observation and explicit owner confirmation that page-table/scratch pages were published; failed reruns clear their corresponding proof. Post-GPU CPU sync requires an armed snapshot and caller-confirmed retirement/reset. Host tests cover translated/changed VT-d, wrong owner, reset gating, cache operation and arming/retirement states; kernel and host builds pass. This remains internal: the owner must hold the device/IOMMU lease continuously, publish page tables, handle GPU-side cache flushes and command security, and expose the real i915 ABI. No Dell deployment occurred.

**Application submission snapshots:** Per-file buffer lookup now resolves all copied handles under one lock, rejects duplicates and retains all objects atomically. `intel_bdw_exec_snapshot.cpp` builds a kernel-owned, sorted snapshot of pinned i915-style objects, checks GPU-address range/alignment, batch bounds and no writable batch, and uses those retained page arrays to build a PPGTT. It accepts a documented limited soft-pinned object subset only; the caller must decode the actual UAPI and reject unsupported relocations, fences and engine features. Once armed, a snapshot refuses release unless its owner proves retirement or reset; caller serializes build/arm/release. Host tests cover handle closure after resolution, duplicate/cross-file handles, sorting, invalid and overlapping addresses, batch checks, PPGTT construction and refusal to release an uncertain submission. The kernel build passes. This does not parse or authorize GPU commands, establish DMA/cache safety, schedule work or expose an i915 ioctl/device; those remain required before any application execution. No Dell deployment occurred.

**Intel buffer chunks and per-file handles:** GPU buffer VMALLOC backing is now divided into at most 256-page chunks, keeping each existing VMM allocation/free critical section bounded; kernel virtual addresses must be obtained per page and are not globally contiguous. Host tests cover a 513-page object, cleanup after a failed later chunk and mapping across chunks. New `intel_bdw_file.cpp` supplies a locked per-open 8,192-slot buffer handle table and opaque, non-reused mmap tokens; lookups retain buffer references, and close releases outside the file lock. Tests cover cross-file isolation, partial mapping bounds, mapping lifetime across handle/file closure and stale-token rejection after handle reuse. These are kernel-built internal facilities only; they are not wired to the existing virtio-gpu DRM node or a new i915 fd/ioctl/mmap route, and no submission or CPU/GPU coherence is implied. Chunking bounds individual VMM lock holds but does not measure latency or solve global VMALLOC metadata/reclaim pressure for many large objects. Guarded kernel and focused host tests pass; not deployed to the Dell.

**Page-backed Intel GPU buffer object:** `intel_bdw_buffer.cpp` is now part of the kernel build. It creates zeroed VMALLOC-backed, page-aligned buffers, records their physical page list (restricted to the current 16 GiB direct-map range), and uses `MappingBacking` references so handles, CPU mappings and GPU pins can independently retain the allocation. A `BdwGpuBufferPin` releases its reference only after the caller explicitly proves retirement; uncertain work keeps it pinned. Host tests exercise allocation failures, zeroing, multiple references, uncertain retention, eventual safe release and building a PPGTT from the buffer's pages. The guarded kernel build passed after reconfiguration with the existing Hack font and freetype-py environment. This is not yet connected to a file/handle table, mmap, DMA admission, cache synchronization or an i915 ioctl; no Intel render node is exposed. Large VMALLOC allocation/free operations currently use existing VMM locking and need latency/scalability review before enabling unrestricted application allocations. No Dell deployment occurred.

**Application address-space groundwork:** The existing DRM render node and sysfs identity are virtio-gpu-specific; Intel still has no application-facing i915 device. The Gen8 PPGTT builder now accepts strictly sorted mappings up to 65,536 pages, limited further by its 128 table-page budget, avoiding its former 1,024-page/quadratic validation constraint for that path while preserving the old unsorted interface. `BdwBuildExecAddressSpace` translates ordered, pinned buffer-page descriptions into the sorted PPGTT image and rejects overflow, overlap, invalid DMA and workspace aliasing. Host tests cover a 1,025-page mapping, actual resulting entries, two discontiguous buffer objects, overlap and failure without modifying the page tables; the existing render/allocator tests and guarded kernel build pass. This is not wired to user handles, an i915 ioctl, a live GPU lease or application submission. Next build per-file buffer ownership and memory mappings, context/execbuffer admission and hardware scheduling, and integrate with the actual Mesa iris/hasvk ABI before attempting GL/Vulkan tests.

**GPU takeover correction:** Ian challenged the earlier assumption that a surviving GGTT entry necessarily requires old RAM to stay reserved across all boot paths. Astra's source review agrees: the entry is a passive translation, and the experiment submitted no work or demonstrated DMA. Intel's [Broadwell memory-view documentation](https://www.x.org/docs/intel/BDW/intel-gfx-prm-osrc-bdw-vol05-memory_views_0.pdf) also identifies display and CPU-aperture consumers, so protection requires knowing whether the particular address can be accessed, not merely whether the render engine is enabled. Linux i915's [early GPU sanitization](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_driver.c#L184) and [GGTT initialization](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/v6.12/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_ggtt.c#L761) provide a practical takeover pattern: reset inherited engine execution, account for active display reservations, replace unallocated mappings with a current-owned scratch page, invalidate, then initialize new submission state. Do not assume prior shutdown succeeds, conflate the stale PTE with active DMA, or claim Linux proves Dell firmware/SMM behavior. The current experimental mapping gate stays closed until a coherent takeover sequence and validation exist; cross-boot permanent RAM reservation on every loader is no longer an assumed prerequisite. The user has been told the earlier framing was too strong.
