The first promotion fixture used an AHCI panic-test kernel that disables ordinary writes and therefore correctly failed before mutation; the ordinary writable test kernel passed.

The matching physical-profile compact recovery candidate is prepared at `build/hardware/dell-torn-journal-recovery-candidate-20261105/`, using the prior identity-bound inventory, pinned checkers and the matching xHCI module; current live identity must be reconfirmed before any physical publication. `tools/hardware_ssd_recovery_stage.c` can stage a new create-only `RECOVNEW` with the replacement build flag, and the new `tools/hardware_recovery_promote.c` validates exact old, new and independent legacy pairs, renames the old alternate to `RECOVBAK`, then renames the staged pair to `RECOV2`, flushing and checking identities and hashes. `scripts/test_recovery_promote_host.py` passes success, both rename failures, and wrong-hash refusal, with an uncertain mutation retaining its lock. Firmware can fall back to legacy RECOVERY in the gap, but that older path does not itself contain the torn-journal fix.

Local panic-journal recovery now accepts a recognizable version-1 but invalid record beside a blank header and writes the next capture to the blank slot, preserving the damaged slot. Both boot-time AHCI admission paths use the same policy; arbitrary nonzero unrecognized contents and two invalid nonblank slots still refuse writes. Standalone journal tests cover either damaged slot and preservation; panic snapshot and AHCI byte-write host tests pass. A fresh nonproduction `BROOK_AHCI_PANIC_TEST` kernel passed disposable TCG/OVMF cases for a torn initial header, unknown corrupt contents, and two normal sequential captures using `scripts/test_panic_ahci_qemu.py`; the torn test independently checked the damaged slot and decoded the new panic packet. This is local, not deployed, and does not cover all possible torn header shapes or actual power loss. The separate guarded desktop and physical FAT-backed journal still need integration validation. Building the non-guarded test kernel also exposed and fixed an unused GPU state variable when automatic recovery is compiled out.

The same nonproduction kernel also passed `scripts/test_panic_fat_qemu.py --case torn-journal`: the FAT-backed mapped file preserved its damaged first slot, recorded the next panic in its second slot, changed no sectors outside the file and passed offline `fsck.fat`. This exercises the production-shared FAT journal mapping admission on a disposable QEMU disk, not the complete guarded desktop or physical SSD.

The local scratch-takeover path now has a hard fail-closed gate: the presence of `/etc/dell-gpu-crossboot-safe` cannot by itself establish cross-boot safety or enable a mapping. The scanout host test verifies that even with both opt-in markers the PTE write and dependent BCS initialization are refused; the GGTT binding host test also passes. This strengthening is local and has not been deployed to the Dell. A cross-boot solution must cover the independently selectable old and F5 loaders as well as the guarded default, and must account for firmware's allocations and GPU activity before Brook gets control; reserving pages in the kernel alone cannot satisfy those requirements. The earlier test of BCS initialization using a fake backend is no longer exercised through this now-disabled production entry point.

**Warm-reset GGTT lifetime issue and cleanup:** The generation-47 scratch PTE `119971841` survived the warm reboot into generation 48 even though its PMM page was only pinned for the previous boot. The attempted scratch takeover on boot `89a8d6df54904244b12a586aa98c951d` refused the already-valid PTE before writing; BCS initialization was not attempted. GPU/display remained idle/healthy. On boot `e7710ceee64449b0a8e6cf9a28544b79`, `gpu-clear-prior-scratch` compared the exact known prior PTE, cleared it, completed translation invalidations and released forcewake; readback was zero, the other seven PTEs and display were unchanged, and the desktop was ready. A checked reboot request `9cac0f979bce4772b3f519426e067762` produced current boot `15aff76aedda4579956934958e6ebf7b`, session `4469df71532343dc9ef1214310d19f11`; the slot still reads zero and desktop is ready. The one-off cleanup command recognizes only the recorded generation-47 value and is not a general solution. No BCS command or accelerated rendering has executed.

Local retained-scratch helpers now initialize and publish the Gen8 status records and read the producer with CPU cache maintenance, but only after the one-way scratch pin. Host tests verify denial before pin, initialized records and producer value after pin; the guarded kernel builds. They perform PMM checks and cannot be invoked while holding the VMM page-table lock, so an engine backend still needs a lock-safe handoff. No hardware HWS or execlist initialization has been attempted. Linux's [Gen8 PAT setup](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/daeinki/drm-exynos/+/61d861cf478576d85d6032f864360a34b26084b1/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gtt.c) describes GT GGTT accesses as selecting PAT entry 0, reinforcing that the existing Dell `0x03` policy cannot simply be changed without accounting for active consumers and cache visibility.

The local VMM now has a restricted single-slot scratch takeover path within the serialized forcewake/page-table critical section. It audits the exact GGTT and flush-control aliases, checks the forcewake ACK, writes only the requested scratch PTE, posts through flush control and invokes the four-engine bounded TLB invalidator. The caller must first establish device admission, pin the scratch and reservation, and exclude display/firmware users; this entry point does not establish those facts itself. Host tests exercise the MMIO wrapper, failed invalidation and existing forcewake/binder behavior, and the guarded kernel builds. There is no production caller or physical test yet; no GGTT write has occurred. Any eventual caller must explicitly account for the unproven firmware/SMM exclusion and preserve the active display.

Local GGTT takeover work now provides a one-way boot-lifetime pin for the retained scratch page and reservation, and a bounded single-slot scratch transaction. The transaction double-reads the prior entry, never replays unknown firmware bits, attempts to drain even a failed posted write, and leaves the slot/page pinned after any attempted store. Host tests cover successful scratch mapping, changed pre-state, failed store and failed invalidation; retained allocation tests verify that the one-way pin prevents release. The guarded kernel builds. No production MMIO owner calls the transaction yet; it is not deployed and no physical GGTT PTE has been written.

The local retained BCS allocation now includes a separately allocated, zeroed and CPU-published GGTT scratch page, distinct from all 19 one-shot pages. Release also refuses if the binder has ever left fresh state: takeover rollback can leave a scratch PTE installed even when one-shot pages themselves are releasable, so scratch and the range must remain pinned. Host tests cover the dedicated page, allocation failure and a failed PTE write followed by scratch rollback; the guarded kernel builds. The backend does not yet use this page, and this change is undeployed.

The local BCS MMIO synchronizer now requires the hardware write cursor to retain its reset value `7` immediately before programming the CSB cursors, and rejects all-ones reads. This guards against a stale reset proof but has not been exercised after real HWS/execlist setup; the physical reset-only observation was `7`. Host one-shot/forcewake tests pass; no production MMIO owner or live submission exists. The observed PAT byte `0x03` is write-back with the zero cache-target encoding, not uncached: [i915 definitions](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/daeinki/drm-exynos/+/3723acbe985227b4268c3ce749309e1e55bfd3d5/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gtt.h) encode WB as 3 and UC as 0. Do not use it as an uncached shortcut around PAT/cache ownership.

The local GGTT allocator also keeps each reservation within one PTE MMIO page, matching the existing binder's access geometry. A fragmented-page host test verifies it skips the remaining 16 entries when asked for 32, and the allocator, binding and one-shot tests pass; the guarded kernel builds. On current Dell boot `160022d779fe4bc29fd17cd9b5c13cbf`, the boot PCI inventory reported graphics control `0x01c1` (GGMS 3, 8 MiB, 1,048,576 entries). This is a captured value, not exclusive device ownership. The allocator change is not deployed and remains preparation for a device backend, not GPU execution.

The local GGTT reservation now derives its upper bound from the captured Broadwell graphics-control GGMS field instead of assuming the entire 8 MiB PTE aperture has backing. The shared reservation space refuses use before one-time sizing and never allocates past that bound. Host tests cover the three nonzero encodings, unavailable configuration, fixed sizing and an exhausted boundary; preparation and scanout host tests pass, and the guarded kernel builds. The decoding follows [Linux i915's Broadwell sizing](https://gbmc.googlesource.com/linux/+/6d0ebb3904853d18eeec7af5e8b4ca351b6f9025/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_ggtt.c) and [field definitions](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/krzk/linux/+/refs/heads/master/include/drm/intel/i915_drm.h). This remains undeployed and does not independently reserve firmware mappings or authorize DMA; any live backend must also revalidate the current device configuration and its lease.

The private RCS preparation plan now includes its indirect workaround batch and scratch as entries 26 and 27 in the same 28-page GGTT lease as the context, ring and status/completion pages. The PMM-only preparation builds the batch in the actual private page, fills the context pointers, initializes scratch, publishes all 37 allocated pages including PPGTT backing, and frees them without device access. Host allocation-failure, context/layout, binding and one-shot tests pass, and the guarded kernel builds. This is still a disposable preparation path: no production GGTT ownership, device mapping, retained render context, default 3D state or submission has been established.

Local Broadwell render-context work now includes a private indirect-context workaround batch builder (`intel_bdw_render_wa.h`) based on [i915's Gen8 workaround sequence](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/gclement/linux/+/9413cd7792dc03608ec9b1f1f5c74fc54e714ed3/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_lrc.c). It requires distinct, non-overlapping GGTT pages for the batch and scratch, emits the arbitration/L3 flush/SLM sequence, and points the prepared RCS context at the two-cacheline batch. Standalone host tests validate commands, context fields and geometry. This is private RAM construction only: the render allocator has not yet reserved or pinned those pages, and no live GPU, context default state, GT workarounds, user ABI, 3D acceleration or physical test is implied.

The local BCS one-shot now revalidates exclusive engine ownership and the PAT lease after binding, before each ELSP dword, after completion, and while consuming/acknowledging context status. A lost lease after binding or during the four-write submission quarantines retained mappings and prevents further port writes; a lost lease during status processing faults before acknowledgment. Host tests exercise each of these transitions and pass; the guarded kernel builds. These checks rely on a future backend to implement a real continuous lease and cannot themselves exclude firmware or establish GPU visibility.

The local GGTT MMIO binder no longer reports invalidation success from the flush-control posting read alone: the owner must additionally invalidate GPU translations, and a failed invalidation quarantines the binding. A new bounded Gen8 invalidator and allowlisted MMIO accessor implement i915's four GT2 engine TLB registers (`0x4260`, `0x4264`, `0x426c`, `0x4270`), writing bit 0 and waiting for each request to clear. Host tests cover a successful sequence, busy registers, failed writes, timeout, permanent uncertainty, bad MMIO and binder quarantine; the guarded kernel builds. See [i915's invalidation logic](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_tlb.c) and [Gen8 register definitions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gt_regs.h). This invalidates engine translation state only: it does not establish active-engine power/forcewake ownership, flush GPU data caches or display translations, or supply the stronger complete PAT-transition guarantee. No production owner calls it and no physical invalidation writes have occurred.

Local BCS preparation now has a PAT-establishment callback before its two stable policy checks. `BdwPatLease` and `BdwPatMmio` implement a constrained candidate transaction: preserve unrelated PAT bytes, verify stable pre-state and approved display/engine transition, update entries 0 and 4, drain/invalidate and double-check, or attempt verified restoration and quarantine uncertain failures. Host tests cover the Dell values, denied transitions, changing pre-state, partial write, failed drain, restoration, allowlisted MMIO and one-shot behavior; the guarded kernel builds. The owner must establish firmware/engine exclusion, display safety and an actual GPU cache/TLB invalidation guarantee, including draining a failed posted write. There is no such production owner or physical PAT write yet; simulated restoration does not prove hardware safety.

The local BCS one-shot now checks the descriptor and two stable private-PAT reads itself, instead of accepting a backend's unqualified Boolean. It admits only the valid legacy 48-bit PPGTT descriptor and the expected i915 index-0/index-4 bytes (`0x07`/`0x0b`); observed Dell values (`0x03`/`0x03`), changed reads, lost lease and all-ones values fail before any GGTT or engine write. The owner still must provide a fresh forcewake-protected PAT read and retain exclusive policy control through submission; a point-in-time boot snapshot is not a lease. Host one-shot/preparation tests pass and the guarded kernel builds. [Intel's Broadwell memory manual](https://kiwitree.net/~lina/intel-gfx-docs/prm/bdw/intel-gfx-prm-osrc-bdw-vol05-memory_views_1.pdf) distinguishes Brook's legacy descriptor from advanced contexts with per-context policy. No production backend or PAT update exists yet; this gate is undeployed.

During the existing opt-in forcewake observation, the additional UC-audited PAT register page was admitted and the two stable samples returned low/high `0x03030303`/`0x03030303`; forcewake was released. See `build/hardware/dell-gpu-pat-physical-20261105/snapshot.json`. Compared with [i915's Broadwell PAT setup](https://cos.googlesource.com/third_party/kernel/+/1f2112af11e4c330cd070464e95ba9f546b8959b/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_gem_gtt.c) and [encoding](https://gbmc.googlesource.com/linux/+/5e0c67998152bdb91b056160449ee542b86271a5/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gtt.h), global entries 0 and 4 are `0x03`, rather than the i915 choices `0x07` and `0x0b`. The snapshot is point-in-time and advanced contexts can carry their own PAT; it does not establish the effective policy during a context or authorize reprogramming the global PAT. The backend's GPU PAT gate must continue to deny submission until the effective policy is established and controlled. Host tests cover page denial, changed samples, forcewake and debug serialization.

The local one-shot submission path now explicitly arms a single validated context descriptor before sending its four ELSP dwords. The BCS MMIO accessor enforces empty second descriptor then first descriptor high/low order, does a status-register posting read after the final write, and refuses reuse or any further write after a mismatch or ownership failure. The order and posting read follow [i915's Gen8 ELSP sequence](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/virt/kvm/kvm/+/c48ec42d6eae08f55685ab660f0743ed33b9f22a/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/intel_lrc.c). Host tests cover valid and invalid order, lost ownership, failed posting read and refusal before a one-shot port write; the guarded kernel builds. This is not a live device backend: the accessor requires a real owner to validate the descriptor and retain mappings, forcewake, cache visibility and retirement. No ELSP writes have been made on the Dell.

The BCS takeover interface now supplies the exact retained HWS page (CPU and DMA addresses) to its backend after GGTT binding; the one-shot host simulation checks that page is the one in the bound PTE. Status initialization now has a reusable page-alignment-checked poison/producer initializer and a checked publication callback. The retained PMM allocator also has CPU cache-publication and producer-read operations for private kernel pages, verifying the direct-map address, tag, owner, reference and mapping counts. Host one-shot and preparation tests pass, as does the guarded kernel build. These methods are groundwork for the hardware owner and have no physical caller; CPU cache flushing does not prove GPU PAT, DMA ownership, coherent device writes or safe submission.

The local one-shot BCS initialization now calls an explicit CSB synchronization step after programming the bound HWS. The MMIO accessor writes and posts the Gen8 status pointer twice around backend status-memory initialization and publication, checks both hardware pointers and the coherent memory producer at slot five, and requires a backend-provided completed-reset proof and exclusive idle ownership. This follows the [i915 status-pointer reset sequence](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/gclement/linux/+/9413cd7792dc03608ec9b1f1f5c74fc54e714ed3/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_lrc.c). Host tests pass for reset denial, unprepared memory, stale producer, restricted registers and the existing one-shot failure cases; the guarded kernel builds, though it has no instantiated production BCS MMIO owner. Neither the reset proof nor the cache-coherent memory callbacks have a real backend, so this remains untested on physical GPU and does not authorize submission.

Local graphics work adds an explicit BCS-only reset sequence and narrow MMIO accessor (`intel_bdw_bcs_reset.h`, `intel_bdw_bcs_mmio.h`). It checks exclusive owner/quiescence, rejects catastrophic or concurrent reset state, requests Gen8 reset readiness, then requests and waits for the BLT reset domain, with bounded waits and an uncertain result after potentially delivered writes. Host tests cover readiness, already-ready, timeout, failed write, competing reset, ownership loss and register allowlisting. Linux i915's [reset sequence](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/clk/linux/+/c1c77b0e07dc6231db3c2c7b847c514849d53b99/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/intel_uncore.c) and [register definitions](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_engine_regs.h) are the reference. No production owner calls this and it has not touched the Dell. A domain acknowledgement alone does not prove CSB cursor synchronization, restore forcewake, release DMA pages or enable GPU submission.

The tested AHCI yield change is now the default Dell desktop payload `dell-ahci-yield-20261105`: private candidate verification passed, and its exact production kernel/initrd passed disposable KVM startup panic, reset, USB retrieval and repair (`build/hardware/guard-ahci-yield-production-qemu-20261105/`). The checked A/B updater activated generation 35 slot 0 and verified the new payload after restart (`build/hardware/dell-ahci-yield-activate-20261105/receipt.json`). New boot `b2de4b454ebb4832a37d5955c91a1e30`, session `1d0bad53ca714d1d9668abff99a998b2`, reports a ready writable desktop. Previous `dell-display-observe-20261105` remains slot 1; F5 and recovery were not replaced. This is a physical boot check, not a physical test of the panic-during-I/O boundary.

AHCI panic handling now refuses to start another ordinary disk command when panic reservation is pending, allowing a long multi-command operation to return and transfer the gate after its current command. The refusal precedes descriptor changes and does not quarantine the device. Host tests exercise yielding after the first write chunk and between the read and write of a partial sector, plus gate races; the guarded kernel builds. An explicitly selected KVM-only test hook held a live writer, then attempted a real additional command after panic requested the gate; it was refused without quarantine, panic took ownership, wrote its packet, reset, and recovery retrieved the identical packet over emulated USB and repaired the volume. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-ahci-yield-qemu-v10-20261105/`. The hook and its fixture must never be deployed. The production change cannot recover capture if the current command or its owner is stuck, or if panic occurs on the owning CPU; the test does not prove physical disk or USB behavior.

After Ian restored connectivity again, physical session `688ad93e3cd247568243e9566e93fb5a` verified the unchanged boot `7389e7824ace4fd897cd8e82b8310b7c` and ready desktop. Locally, a narrowly allowlisted BCS MMIO accessor now implements the register interface used by the existing execlist initialization sequence; host tests exercise initialization, denied register/value writes, ownership loss, HWS validation and unsynchronized CSB refusal. It is not wired to a production owner or deployed and cannot establish forcewake, engine ownership or reset synchronization by itself. The corresponding host one-shot and GGTT binder tests pass.

The Dell was reattached after Ian restored connectivity; session `f20c72ba6a0e45f8af03139e195860f3` verifies the same boot `b8913a47b3aa42aca88c8e1de6a1f8f7` and a ready desktop. Ian asked for USB reliability and diagnosis after the recovery and graphics goal. Linux i915's [GGTT initialization](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_ggtt.c) reserves preallocated regions before clearing allocator holes; its Gen8 clear writes scratch PTEs, rather than replaying arbitrary old PTEs. Its [driver probe](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_driver.c) removes conflicting aperture owners before GGTT initialization, and its [display initialization](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/display/intel_display_driver.c) reconstructs BIOS framebuffer state. This supports an explicit takeover design, but does not establish that Brook has found every live display/firmware reservation, that the sampled eight entries are free, or that SMM will leave the GPU alone. The existing software allocator and stable reads alone are insufficient to authorize writes; retain the fail-closed behavior until takeover, scratch mapping, ordered PTE publication and GPU TLB invalidation are implemented and validated.

Recovery diagnostics now retain boot-pinned snapshots of both validated journal slots, and `hw_recovery_panic` accepts `previous=true` to retrieve the older one through the existing checksum-verified bridge. The original command remains unchanged; an absent, corrupt or ambiguous older record is not presented as valid. Host journal, normal snapshot, recovery/normal debug-command, restricted-policy and loopback bridge tests pass; guarded, recovery-only and normal kernels build. A disposable KVM repair-to-guarded-desktop fixture seeded two validated records and retrieved both exact payloads and sequence numbers through the bridge during restricted recovery and again after desktop handoff; evidence is `build/hardware/guard-two-panic-qemu-v5-20261105/`. The first fixture attempt used a production kernel without the test-only bridge-window marker and failed in the test harness. A later run discovered that restricted recovery did not allow the new command; the policy was fixed before the passing run.

The exact tested guarded desktop kernel and Dell initrd candidate `dell-dual-panic-20261105` were verified and activated as generation 33, slot 0, using the checked A/B updater; receipt `build/hardware/dell-dual-panic-activate-20261105/receipt.json` reports `boot_verified`. The previous desktop remains slot 1. One deliberately requested physical panic on boot `fd90404b4f3d4aa3b68ddb4827dea632` was captured as sequence 2 (1716 bytes, CRC `1b894f59`); recovery boot `87f8d7057d7947138612df2425ad2c18` exposed the packet and performed ext2 repair, then reset to ready guarded desktop boot `63071fe94cfa4b2399c0aa2c7abdf3e6`, session `358a0c20be094e7a8e2a1fa914d605a0`. On that desktop both sequence 2 and the earlier sequence 1 were retrieved with checksums. Sequence 1 matches the previously saved packet byte-for-byte; sequence 2 decodes against the exact candidate kernel as `SHELL: dell-dual-panic-test` and contains a log tail. Evidence: `build/hardware/dell-dual-panic-physical-20261105/`. The first attempt to prepare the RAM-only test script used an absent executable and failed before process creation; the second completed, and the panic dispatch was sent only once. The separate physical recovery-only image remains the older build and exposes only the newest record; it was not updated. This provides another successful planned panic/recovery cycle, not proof of arbitrary hangs or power-loss durability, and does not add panic-time networking.

On the same desktop boot, a checked store-path inventory found only the yquake2 and OpenAL packages missing from the 310-path game closure; the selected Vulkan tools closure lacked four packages. Their approximately 10 MB archive was uploaded using transaction `c6f05db4b43f4b4eaa3cc1f00719ac23` and extracted into `/nix/store/.brook-gpu-stage-c6f05db4`; all 46 regular-file SHA-256 hashes and 17 symlink targets matched, and a guest `sync` completed. The archive and manifests are in `build/hardware/dell-gpu-workloads-20261105/`. Automatic review rejected publishing the six packages at their canonical `/nix/store` paths because of the broader persistent system mutation; do not bypass that rejection. The staged copies may be used directly with explicit library paths. Staged `vulkaninfo --summary` loaded with the staged Vulkan loader and Wayland libraries and forced the existing Intel HasVK ICD, but returned `ERROR_INITIALIZATION_FAILED` because no valid GPU was detected (job `800458ff922743ccbf55a01aa7eedf89`). A copy of the existing yquake2 GL wrapper adjusted to use the staged paths and `/data/home/quake2/baseq2/pak0.pak` was uploaded as boot-RAM artifact `bd305cd55aba4ff5a55098f011df6078`; job `3f5f3dcee5a747908954bd9765d0eaab` launched its GL3 renderer with an Iris override and `+quit`. It initialized the renderer and game data but explicitly identified `GL_RENDERER: llvmpipe`, so this is a software fallback baseline, not hardware acceleration or gameplay proof. The staged binary also reported its compiled-in canonical share directory and `yq2.cfg` missing, and OpenAL/ALSA initialization failed; these are additional test-setup issues to resolve before claiming full game acceptance. Complete job output is saved locally as `yquake2-gl-baseline.json` and `vulkaninfo-baseline.json` in the workload evidence directory. The wrapper artifact is lost on reboot and must be transferred again rather than assumed persistent.

The local GGTT transaction has an additional explicitly authorized takeover path: it compares unknown pre-existing PTEs without replaying them and restores touched entries to a pinned scratch page, including after partial write failure. The backend must independently prove ownership of the exact range and preserve scratch-page DMA accessibility for as long as those PTEs survive; failed ordering or invalidation quarantines referenced memory. A working-state guard also rejects reentrant calls during the transaction. The BCS one-shot now exposes this path using a scratch page owned by its backend, with the same double-snapshot, admission and submission gates; its ordinary path continues to reject unknown high bits. It additionally rejects scratch DMA aliases with any of the 19 retained pages, including PPGTT and batch pages not present in the eight-slot GGTT lease. Host transaction and one-shot tests pass, including every retained-page alias, the Dell's high-bit samples, takeover refusal, delayed writes and failed invalidation. Neither path has a production backend or has modified the Dell. On current boot `63071fe94cfa4b2399c0aa2c7abdf3e6`, BCS again sampled idle in legacy submission mode; after explicitly triggering the deferred VT-d sample, the retained-page DMA-conditions snapshot returned status 0. These observations do not authorize DMA. Actual display/firmware takeover, scratch lifetime, MMIO/TLB operations and engine initialization remain to be implemented. Linux's [Gen8 GGTT invalidation](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_ggtt.c) orders its write-combined PTE stores with an uncached flush-control register write; Brook's different uncached mapping and any required posting/engine synchronization still need a verified implementation.

The local BCS takeover path now binds its status page before calling backend execlist initialization, rather than requiring firmware to have already enabled the mode. `intel_bdw_bcs_init.h` expresses the Broadwell HWSTAM, run-list mode, stop-ring and HWS register sequence from Linux [i915 initialization](https://kernel.googlesource.com/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/hyperv/linux/+/0072a0c14d5b7cb72c611d396f143f5dcd73ebe2/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/intel_lrc.c), with readbacks and explicit ownership/CSB preconditions. It also requires the backend to prove the hardware CSB cursor and software cursor are synchronized after HWS programming: writing the memory copy to five alone is insufficient because Linux's corresponding initialization assumes a reset engine. Host simulation demonstrates transition from legacy mode and quarantines the retained pages if synchronization or any of the seven register operations fails before submission. Existing one-shot and GGTT host tests pass and the guarded kernel builds. The helper has no real MMIO backend and is exercised only by the fake backend; it has not changed hardware, proven cache/PAT, claimed an engine, or executed a blit. Implement and validate those missing operations before attempting physical submission.

`intel_bdw_ggtt_mmio.h` now provides direct volatile 64-bit PTE reads/writes and a fenced flush-control write/posting read for a single already-audited GGTT page, constrained to a contiguous lease and delegated owner checks. The existing `VmmDellReservedGgttCriticalRead` path now instantiates this accessor for its real read-only diagnostic under the existing VMM lock and UC alias checks; its local owner explicitly denies lease validation and writes. Host tests exercise the accessor against ordinary memory, including read-only authorization, bounds and lost ownership; the guarded kernel builds. This updated read path is local and undeployed. There is still no write-capable production owner or caller: the VMM must audit and hold the flush-register mapping, establish device ownership, pin scratch/backing pages, and verify that the flush operation has the required Broadwell ordering/invalidation semantics before physical writes. Host memory tests cannot establish MMIO or GPU behavior, and no new PTE write or GPU command has been performed on the Dell.

The guarded desktop exposes `bridge hardware gpu-display-state`, a stable double-read of primary, sprite and cursor control/surface registers for the three Broadwell display pipes. Register locations follow Linux's [primary plane](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/display/i9xx_plane_regs.h), [sprite and cursor register definitions](https://code.googlesource.com/linux/torvalds/linux/+/586b5dfb51b962c1b6c06495715e4c4f76a7fc5a/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/i915_reg.h). The read requires armed panic reset, the matching Dell GPU identity and D0, admitted MMIO pages and current-CPU UC alias checks. Host evidence, instability and denial tests pass, as does the guarded kernel build. The exact kernel passed disposable repair/handoff and dual-panic retrieval (`build/hardware/guard-display-observe-qemu-20261105/`), then physical candidate `dell-display-observe-20261105` activated generation 34, slot 1 and booted verified (receipt `build/hardware/dell-display-observe-activate-20261105/receipt.json`); the prior dual-panic desktop remains slot 0. Current boot is `7389e7824ace4fd897cd8e82b8310b7c`, session `581dce8f6b104911bad5cd2dc0d60fae`. Two snapshots agreed: pipe A primary control `0x98000000`, stride 12800, surface/live 0; all sampled sprite/cursor and pipe B/C values zero (`build/hardware/dell-display-observe-physical-20261105/snapshot.json`). Pipe A is consistent with an enabled, linear 32-bit framebuffer at GGTT offset zero. Powered-down domains can read zero, so this does not prove B/C are disabled or fully describe plane extents, firmware ownership or SMM behavior. It must not be used alone to authorize takeover.

Physical recovery milestone: the Dell's preallocated inactive update slot was activated with `dell-guarded-desktop-panic-v2-20261105`; receipt `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-v2-activate-20261105/receipt.json` records generation 26, slot 1, checked restart and verified payload ID. Boot `76901fe010724b57a55b06a027c3a514` completed the FAT guard check, pinned and armed the panic journal, mounted the desktop, and reported `GUARD_DESKTOP_PANIC_RESET armed=1`. A deliberately requested physical panic through the boot-RAM shell script reset the Dell; recovery boot `aa38b1244cbc409a84bc2cdc2505000c` exposed sequence 1, 1767 bytes, CRC `74f6e76c` through the restricted debug bridge. It automatically rebooted again to guarded desktop boot `7ec1323aca624bd1875e420c8698085e`, session `ee8ffe2b13b94e9583d89b54bc8d9b8b`, reporting the same prior packet, a ready desktop and reset armed. The packet was read from the new boot, CRC checked and decoded against the exact candidate kernel: `build/hardware/dell-guarded-panic-physical-20261105/panic.bin` and `panic.json`; its message is `SHELL: dell-recovery-physical-test`. The temporary recovery boot did not provide the desktop compositor; the final boot reports a live compositor and desktop. This proves one planned physical panic/reset/journal/recovery cycle, not hard-hang recovery, repeated reliability, arbitrary power-loss durability, or every firmware path. The first debug `exec` from a process `/tmp` path returned without a panic; the successful script was on boot RAM. Ian witnessed the panic and the intermediate blank desktop, and has been informed it was intentional.

The optional VT-d diagnostic has a new deferred mode (`/etc/dell-gpu-vtd-probe` containing `2\n`): the boot only records the request, and a later `bridge hardware gpu-vtd sample` attempts the read on the BSP only after panic reset is armed. Existing identity, DMAR and memory-type gates remain; host tests cover unarmed, wrong-CPU, successful and failed one-shot paths. This is observation, not GPU DMA admission. A matched Dell candidate `build/hardware/dell-vtd-deferred-candidate-20261105/` passed private selector/module checks and a disposable KVM repair-to-desktop fixture (`build/hardware/guard-vtd-deferred-qemu-20261105/`). Its physical update receipt `build/hardware/dell-vtd-deferred-activate-20261105/receipt.json` records activation as generation 27, slot 0, a checked restart and verified new payload. After Ian restored the network the original updater completed with `boot_verified`; the current boot is `711a81731c94427a8dea1d946c41d1e0`, session `9e47f378edd84607841affba2afe9d4f`. The guarded deferred read succeeded: version 0x10, GSTS 0 (translation disabled), capability 0x1c0000c40660462 and PMEN 0 (protected memory disabled/status clear). This is a point-in-time observation, not exclusive DMA or firmware ownership. The previous guarded desktop remains the other slot.

An optional BCS allocation retains the existing one-shot object's 19 PMM pages and its allocator for the lifetime of the boot; explicit release is allowed only while the one-shot remains safely prepared. Allocation and cache-publication failure release what can safely be released. The `/etc/dell-gpu-retain-bcs` diagnostic opt-in and debug status expose preparation without mapping or submitting anything. Host tests cover retention, duplicate requests, release, allocation failure and publication failure, and the guarded kernel builds. This is resource-lifetime groundwork; it has no production execution backend and is not hardware 3D.

The retained BCS allocation and a fresh DMA-conditions snapshot are now deployed on the Dell. The first version refused the check because the debug worker ran off the BSP; a follow-up permits any CPU while the VMM read itself disables interrupts and checks that CPU's alias and memory type. Candidate `dell-bcs-anycpu-20261105` passed host tests, private pair verification and disposable KVM repair/handoff (`build/hardware/guard-bcs-anycpu-qemu-20261105/`) and booted physically via receipt `build/hardware/dell-bcs-anycpu-activate-20261105/receipt.json`. Current boot `f78bc4b2934043e78490eca0d42eaed6`, session `79562c9c5f8f4356aeb473e61efb3d4e`, reports retained preparation successful, a fresh VT-d sample with translation and protected memory disabled, and `gpu_bcs_dma_snapshot_api` status 0. The check validates kernel ownership, single references, no user mappings and stable VT-d reads; it explicitly does not authorize DMA or establish exclusive firmware/device ownership. No GPU command has been submitted.

The local BCS preparation now obtains its eight GGTT slots from a shared software reservation space instead of assuming a fixed unowned index. Reservations have unique lifetime tokens, cannot overlap, and are returned only after the existing one-shot state permits page release; ambiguous allocation ownership is quarantined. The first 65,536 entries are excluded from allocation. Host tests exercise reservation exhaustion, stale tokens, reuse, page-allocation failure and existing bind/one-shot paths; the guarded kernel builds. This allocator does not inspect or change device PTEs, reserve resources from firmware, or establish driver serialization. The future hardware binder must validate the actual PTEs and preserve display/firmware ownership; the next checkpoint records the later deployment.

The software reservation and an opt-in read-only inspection of its eight GGTT entries have since been deployed as `dell-bcs-ggtt-20261105`; the guarded desktop verified after restart (receipt `build/hardware/dell-bcs-ggtt-activate-20261105/receipt.json`). On boot `f83d2d4297c84a169eb473cfa3529858`, session `481bcee66b9743a395e5b2364915a7f2`, two independently requested snapshots matched: `ba141f3d556fc1ca`, `45ebe0c2aa903e35`, `3a149f3dd56f41ca`, `c5ab60822ad0be75`, `3a549f7dd52f418a`, `c5ab60822ad0be75`, `3a5c9f75d5274182`, `c523600a2a58befd`. These are nonzero with unexpected high bits; stability is not proof of valid PTEs, free space, or ownership. The existing binder expects zero and therefore must refuse this range. No GGTT entry was modified. The snapshot gates on the current retained software lease, reset arming, exact live PCI identity/D0, boot-memory classification and current-CPU UC mappings; it reads the fixed eight entries twice. Host tests cover denial and changing reads, and the exact kernel passed disposable guarded KVM handoff (`build/hardware/guard-bcs-ggtt-qemu-20261105/`). Explain the values and establish firmware/device ownership before binding any range.

The next candidate adds a guarded live double-read of the known firmware-framebuffer GGTT endpoints as a control for the unexpected reserved-entry values. Host tests passed, the private pair was verified, and a disposable KVM repair/handoff passed (`build/hardware/guard-gop-ggtt-qemu-20261105/`). Physical updater receipt `build/hardware/dell-gop-ggtt-activate-20261105/receipt.json` records activation generation 32, slot 1, transaction `9c735ccb34d4426da074699bd921fd67` and committed restart request `e634ca6c8df747f2ad7ec06a2224531a`; its 180-second verification ended `needs_inspection` without a new boot identity. Ian restored the Dell; the new boot `b8913a47b3aa42aca88c8e1de6a1f8f7`, session `7deb55790e584d50ae3316ba4453831b`, reports the exact `dell-gop-ggtt-20261105` payload and a ready writable desktop. Do not replay the historical update or restart. The guarded live framebuffer control returned `0xdd800001` for entry 0 and `0xdedf8001` for entry 5624: their address fields differ by exactly 5624 pages. The eight candidate entries match the prior snapshot. This supports the read path but does not prove the candidate range is unowned or safe to replace. The previous guarded candidate remains in the other slot and F5/recovery remain on the ESP.

Locally the BCS one-shot transaction now captures stable pre-existing GGTT entries only after its backend asserts exclusive handoff, page admission, cache/PAT readiness and lease validation; the binder rechecks them immediately before mutation and can restore them. It conservatively refuses values with bits above the 39-bit device address range, including the Dell's observed candidate values, rather than replaying unverified bits during rollback. Host tests cover a valid nonzero old mapping, unstable samples and changes between snapshot and bind, the actual observed high-bit pattern, and zero writes on refusal. The guarded kernel builds. There is still no physical execution backend or exclusive handoff, and this change is not deployed; it does not establish the odd entries' meaning or hardware 3D.

After the current recovery and graphics goal, Ian wants focused work on Dell USB reliability or at least a diagnosis of the repeated failures. Preserve this as the next follow-up rather than diverting the current goal. The failures have included loss of USB Ethernet and, on some boots, keyboard/touchpad; a full power pull has restored input previously. The cause is not yet established.

On Dell boot `711a81731c94427a8dea1d946c41d1e0`, the existing read-only PCH watchdog diagnostic returned TCO1 control `0x1800`, status2 `0`, timer `4`, and SMI enable `0x80022033`; live ACPI base remained `0x1800` and RCBA configuration was `0xfed1c001`. Intel's [9-series PCH datasheet](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/datasheets/9-series-chipset-pch-datasheet.pdf) defines control bit 11 as timer halt and bit 12 as locking TCO_EN; TCO_EN and global SMI enable are set in the observed SMI register. Thus the timer was halted and firmware had locked the TCO SMI setting at this observation. This does not prove the watchdog cannot be started, whether SMM will service it, or whether reset is inhibited; do not arm it until the latter ownership and reset questions are resolved. A wholly wedged machine still has no proven independent watchdog.

Recovery now opens its existing bounded panic-retrieval window for a dirty desktop crash as well as an interrupted repair, provided a validated previous packet and configured network interface are available. In disposable QEMU, a guarded desktop panic captured its packet and reset; recovery booted with emulated xHCI USB Ethernet, exposed the identical sequence/CRC/bytes through the restricted bridge before starting repair attempt one, then repaired and reset. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-desktop-panic-usb-retrieval-20261105/`. An interrupted-repair regression also passed (`guard-repair-panic-usb-window-regression-20261105/`). An earlier injection immediately after the Dell startup script collided with active AHCI I/O: the panic writer reported `PANIC_DISK_BUSY` and reset without a packet (`guard-dell-desktop-panic-usb-retrieval-20261105/desktop-attempt-serial.log`). The successful retrieval test instead injected before startup I/O. This is an important remaining capture limitation; neither result establishes physical USB, reset or SSD durability. The window and new recovery kernel are undeployed.

The Dell-initrd guarded QEMU shutdown fixture also passed using its xHCI module and emulated USB CDC-ECM Ethernet, with the Dell asynchronous TCP settings retained. It verified xHCI network registration, one debug listener, the Wayland protocol client, checked shutdown with a clean data session, independent FAT/ext2 checks, and provider/client return on the subsequent snapshot boot. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-usb-shutdown-verified-20261105/`. This uses emulated USB and a prior extracted Wayland provider with a synthetic second service; it does not explain the physical Dell's intermittent USB failures or establish physical reset or storage durability.

The virtio-net driver now supplies the network stack's optional nonblocking `tryTransmit` operation. It takes the TX lock only if immediately available, returns `EAGAIN` without publishing when the sole buffer is busy, and retains the DMA buffer after an accepted frame until a valid completion is reaped. Host tests cover lock contention, pending ownership, late completion and corrupt completion quarantine. The Dell-initrd guarded QEMU fixture now keeps its asynchronous TCP markers enabled with the rebuilt virtio module: the bridge completed its checked shutdown, the real extracted Wayland provider and client shut down and returned on the snapshot boot, and offline filesystem checks passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-async-shutdown-20261105/`. This resolves the emulated virtio path's earlier unsupported-operation error; it does not establish physical USB NIC behavior or change the installed Dell driver.

`DebugTcpSpawn` now uses an atomic single-instance guard: the automatic-recovery listener and the Dell startup script's `set wm` no longer create competing listeners, and an initial socket/bind/listen or thread-creation failure permits a later retry. In disposable QEMU using the Dell initrd/script, an extracted Wayland provider, a protocol client and a synthetic second service, the bridge reported one listener; checked shutdown stopped the provider cleanly, finalized the ext2 session, and a snapshot boot of the same verified disk restarted the provider and completed the client exchange. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-shutdown-v4-20261105/`. Earlier fixture runs produced duplicate listeners and TCP send errors (`guard-dell-real-provider-shutdown-v2-20261105/`). The passing fixture also removed Dell-specific experimental TCP markers for its emulated virtio NIC, so it does not isolate which earlier network setting caused the send errors. Host-side snapshot reboot is not a physical power cycle; the other Dell services and physical debug bridge remain unverified. This fix is undeployed and the previously prepared Dell candidate predates it.

The guarded Dell-initrd QEMU fixture now runs a small UID-1000 Wayland client against the extracted real provider. After repair and handoff the client connected to `/tmp/wayland-0`, received registry globals and a `wl_display.sync` callback, then exited successfully; FAT/ext2 checks and the separate synthetic service witness also passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-client-v2-20261105/`. The first fixture client faulted due to an incorrectly aligned hand-written entry stack (`build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-client-20261105/`); aligning it before the C call resolved that fixture error. The provider and runtime are from a prior Dell application extraction, the other service is synthetic, and this protocol exchange does not render a window, exercise the Intel GPU, or prove physical behavior.

The Dell-initrd guarded QEMU fixture also ran an actual Wayland provider extracted from the earlier Dell application tree (`nix/bin/waylandd`, SHA-256 `478e4e732e8c71e237d82d54a2da9efde20d27aba4af6c33d3cb7fc75ddde347`) with its pinned glibc, Wayland and libffi runtime files. After automatic repair and checked handoff, it loaded, listened on `wayland-0` and advertised globals; the two other service paths remained synthetic UID-1000 witnesses. Offline FAT/ext2 checks passed. Evidence and component hashes: `build/hardware/guard-dell-real-provider-20261105/`. The provider was extracted from the earlier application tree, not independently shown to be the executable currently selected by `/nix/profile/bin/waylandd` on the Dell. No GPU backend was present in this fixture; it does not test a real client, the other Dell services, physical boot, or reset.

The exact guarded candidate kernel and Dell initrd were exercised through repair-to-desktop in disposable QEMU with the Dell's original `INIT.RC` preserved (SHA-256 `957c606127fd3ce1e9b7d021b2bd3c5437bc2bd082ab78a8b1f3b8511b890e45`). The fixture rewrote the ATA and partition selectors to the QEMU disk and substituted tiny UID-1000 service executables for `waylandd`, `hardware-dbus`, and `hardware-message`; it retained and launched the initrd's real `HWSTATUS.ELF`. All four launches, checked handoff, a synced service witness, unchanged guard/journal and independent filesystem checks passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-dell-initrd-startup-verified-20261105/`. This uses a modified, compacted initrd, synthetic services and a synthetic data filesystem: it does not prove the real Dell services, hardware drivers, SSD or physical reset work.

Added a private-file verifier for guarded desktop candidates, `scripts/verify_guarded_desktop_candidate.py`. Against the exact prepared Dell pair it checked explicit kernel/source/reference hashes, the guarded/reset build flags and compile evidence (including shutdown and disabled test hooks), FAT consistency, matching source/reference selectors and pinned checkers, unchanged startup script, and source module inventory with matching build-module bytes and ABI. Evidence: `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-private-verify-20261105.json`. Four synthetic FAT tests passed, including altered selectors, script, module, test flag and shutdown undef. The verifier checks selected files rather than proving every other initrd byte is unchanged; build metadata and reference images are evidence, not attestation. It does not establish firmware entrypoints, current physical identity, successful Dell boot or installation authority.

On current pinned Dell boot `70146d8ac9ff4467ad99969561842ade`, read-only AHCI observations match the private guarded desktop candidate's controller BDF and ID, ATA port/model/serial and sector geometry. Boot-pinned sector reads also matched its disk and partition GUIDs, both partition ranges and ext2 UUID; the primary GPT header and complete 128-entry array CRCs passed, and the two expected partition types were the only populated entries. The ext2 superblock magic was present. Evidence is `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-current-identity-20261105.json`; only hashes and check results are saved there. These are observations on this boot, not a filesystem integrity check, SSD cache durability proof or authorization to install. Firmware entrypoint inventory and safe activation remain unresolved.

Prepared a private guarded desktop candidate at `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-private-candidate-20261105/` using the Dell normal desktop initrd, current guarded kernel with `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP_RESET=ON` and `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP_RESET_TEST=OFF`, and matching ABI-65 modules. The original desktop startup script, ATA target, ESP/data selectors, and pinned FAT/ext2 checkers were verified unchanged; those selectors and checker bytes also match the previously prepared Dell recovery candidate. The exact kernel/initrd pair rejected a foreign QEMU SATA disk before guard reservation, and the private disk hash was unchanged; evidence `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-foreign-20261105.log`. This pair was assembled privately using the generic kernel-pair preparer and separate flag/input checks, not the recovery-only preparer or a purpose-built guarded-desktop verifier. Its selectors were subsequently compared with current-boot observations as noted above; the candidate has not been installed or physically booted. The QEMU rejection is not a successful desktop or physical reset test. Firmware entrypoint inventory and a safe migration remain prerequisites to activation.

Added default-off `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP_RESET`, separate from and mutually exclusive with the QEMU-only reset hook. After checked ESP publication, panic journal arming, identity-bound data admission and the dirty desktop mount, it asks the existing platform reset plan to arm; unsupported or disabled reset plans remain unarmed. Shutdown disarms before final sync. The existing recovery-only pair preparer rejects this option in both build cache and compile flags. In disposable QEMU, the new option (without the test selector) captured a panic, delayed, reset and recovered the packet and dirty volume; a real stalled-vCPU test also captured the watchdog reason and reset after the full interval. An injected final-sync panic stayed halted for seven seconds and the subsequent recovery boot repaired the volume. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-reset-candidate-panic-v2-20261105/`, `guard-auto-desktop-reset-candidate-watchdog-20261105/`, and `guard-auto-desktop-reset-candidate-shutdown-v3-20261105/`. An earlier shutdown test exposed a missing disarm preprocessor guard and reset unexpectedly; its preserved evidence is `guard-auto-desktop-reset-candidate-shutdown-v2-20261105/`, and the guard was corrected before the passing tests. Nine recovery-pair preparer tests passed. This option is not deployed and QEMU reset success does not establish Dell firmware entrypoint safety, actual physical resets, cache durability or an independent watchdog. A software watchdog still cannot recover an all-CPU stall.

A fresh guarded-desktop kernel was built with `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP_RESET_TEST=OFF`. On disposable QEMU disks its fixture passed repair-to-desktop service handoff; a separate panic captured the journal, remained halted, and a fresh recovery boot retained the packet and repaired ext2. The same unarmed behavior held when the QEMU-only reset request was explicitly supplied: the compiled-out hook did not arm. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-no-test-handoff-20261105/`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-no-test-panic-20261105/`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-no-test-request-20261105/`. The private pair remains a synthetic QEMU fixture; this does not provide a Dell desktop initrd, enable physical desktop reset, establish safe firmware entrypoints, or replace the recovery preparer's refusal of guarded-desktop kernels.

`nix/experiment-packages.nix` now exports its existing `launchers` derivation separately, allowing the actual wrapper package to be built directly. The build completed as `/nix/store/s1ly2x8h87p9vbns60jqszazik4wjl8a-brook-experiment-launchers`; both generated yquake2 scripts pass `bash -n`, preserve inherited Mesa paths, select their intended GL/software default, and reference their respective built game and OpenAL packages. A closure query confirmed those references and the build's Mesa dependency. The store result was built with `--no-out-link`, is not a GC root, and is not staged on the Dell. Building this combined launcher derivation also pulled other desktop dependencies; its existence does not verify the Dell has the data files, ABI compatibility, or working graphics.

The yquake2 wrapper template now preserves an inherited desktop Mesa DRI/GBM/EGL selection, using its substituted Mesa package paths only when those variables are unset or empty. Eight wrapper tests passed, including inherited and default paths and the existing renderer/argument behavior. `nix/experiment-packages.nix` is the actual generator; the template's older `prestage_yquake2.sh` reference was stale. The updated package is not installed on the Dell, and no GL rendering was tested. A host-side extracted application tree contains older wrappers under `build/hardware/dell-app-migration-20261103/nix/bin/`, but this alone does not establish a complete or installed Dell game closure.

On Dell boot `cf4b013a47334fe5afbd7a7a34dde6d2`, read-only jobs `c524fee2074e441980f10dcadab51a86` and `8b18810942c043aeacfe3ed70fd7f415` did not find the GL launcher, vkcube, vulkaninfo, a render node, or game data at the standard paths; the HasVK profile manifest exists. A subsequent read-only job `3538c7cdc3a24d1789b11f507419bdcd` found the previously staged game engine and `pak0.pak` under `/data/home/quake2`. The yquake2 launcher now accepts `BROOK_QUAKE2_DATA_DIR` so it can use that existing data, retaining `/data/games/quake2` by default; nine host launcher tests pass. The updated launcher package was built locally as `/nix/store/vamd73wxn9zsd5phgdavprwryxns8m0j-brook-experiment-launchers` and both generated scripts pass `bash -n`. It is not GC-rooted or installed on the Dell; the Intel DRM execution backend and actual hardware rendering remain absent.

Local uncommitted Intel work replaces the fixed three-entry one-shot PPGTT construction with a reusable, caller-supplied four-level Gen8 image builder. It validates page alignment, address bounds, table/data aliasing, duplicate virtual mappings and capacity before changing any output; fills absent mappings with the existing read-only scratch hierarchy; and supports mappings in distinct page-table branches. The existing BCS one-shot preparation now uses it. Host tests cover multiple levels, writable/read-only leaves, scratch entries and unchanged output on rejected inputs; the existing one-shot test and a test-kernel build pass. Its layout and cached entries follow Linux's [Gen8 PPGTT definitions](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_gtt.h) and [entry encoding](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/gen8_ppgtt.c). The builder only writes private CPU memory: page pinning, IOMMU access, cache policy, publishing, engine ownership, command submission and an i915 DRM backend remain necessary. It has not run on the Dell.

The Intel work now also constructs a private Broadwell RCS register template in a full 20-page context, with RCS register offsets and posted LRI layout based on Linux's [Gen8 logical context setup](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/torvalds/linux/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_lrc.c) and [render context size](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/gpu/drm/i915/gt/intel_engine_cs.c). Host tests check the layout, 20-page ring/context overlap, invalid DMA and unchanged outputs; the existing BCS tests and test-kernel build pass. This is not a runnable 3D context: engine initialization, hardware workarounds, default GPU state, memory ownership, submission and retirement are still absent. It has not touched physical GPU state.

The private GGTT transaction now admits up to 32 pages, enough to keep the 20-page render context, four-page ring, status page and completion page together. A render-plan builder constructs that 26-page lease and context from caller-supplied DMA pages, rejecting duplicates, alias with the PML4, invalid alignment/ranges and the reviewed Dell reserved-memory window before changing outputs. Host tests bind and retire the plan through the existing fake backend; the enlarged transaction tests exercise failure at every page and delayed writes. These are ownership plans and a simulated transaction, not real reservations, DMA mappings or render submission.

The private render preparation path now allocates 35 PMM pages, builds the render lease and PPGTT from those pages, copies the context to its page backing, performs CPU cache publication, then frees the private pages without GPU access. CPU publication was extended to 64 pages. Host tests cover every PMM allocation failure, cache-publication refusal, successful preparation, and an opt-in `/etc/dell-gpu-render-prepare-only` discovery path including heap failures; `bridge hardware gpu-gop-plan` reports the new requested/built fields. This flag is not present in the deployed Dell image and the diagnostic has not run there. Even on a successful future run it would prove private preparation only, not DMA accessibility or rendering.

The non-virtio desktop environment now selects the Dell's observed Mesa 26.0.6 DRI, GBM and EGL vendor directories when the Iris, GBM and EGL-manifest files all resolve as regular files; otherwise it retains the previous paths. The virtio environment is unchanged, and non-virtio still does not force a Vulkan ICD. A read-only boot-pinned Dell job `8068f6b1e4b648aaafadc8f9a4d32b55` confirmed those three files resolve. Host environment tests and three disposable direct-SATA QEMU boots passed: a synthetic complete closure with an Iris symlink selected the alternate paths, while absent and incomplete closures kept the fallback. Evidence: `build/hardware/gpu-env-dell-mesa-{present,absent,incomplete}-20261105.log`. This is a fixed path to the currently observed package, not general Nix closure discovery; the fallback can still point to an unavailable package. The change is undeployed, does not verify driver dependencies or Vulkan discovery, and does not implement physical i915 execution.

Read-only jobs on the still-current Dell boot `70146d8ac9ff4467ad99969561842ade` found Mesa 26.0.6 Iris, the HasVK ICD manifest, its library and the Mesa EGL vendor manifest under `/nix/store/9kypdl7xqn01sis0ly591wmnsa7hm509-mesa-26.0.6`. The `/nix/store/b793hmy0383vxaax7hiaslzmizzd3pmg-mesa-26.0.6` Iris and HasVK paths hard-coded in the current source's desktop environment were absent on the Dell. Jobs `090e5cb971304fac93906bd9a5c88ab3`, `8a707e9d9cd9410caae5e68517c3eed9`, and `f14811936bb74c6aa416a0a408c727b2` completed with exit zero and output EOF. Their bounded glob search did not find the expected `/nix/bin/brook-yquake2-gl`, a `yquake2` executable directly under a store package's `bin`, or `vkcube`/`vulkaninfo` in that location; other paths were not searched. Mesa identifies Iris as its Gen8-and-newer OpenGL driver in its [source tree guide](https://docs.mesa3d.org/sourcetree.html); its [22.3 release notes](https://docs.mesa3d.org/relnotes/22.3.0.html) record removing Gen7/8 from ANV and adding HasVK. Thus future Broadwell Vulkan tests need HasVK, not the newer Intel ICD alone. File presence is not proof the dependencies load or the GPU executes. The deployed build's actual launch environment was not captured, and current source is undeployed; select paths based on the target's staged closure rather than copying the QEMU store path. The system still lacks a physical i915 DRM backend.

An armed same-CPU nested panic now attempts to halt peers before invoking the reset timer, including when re-entry happens before the original panic reached its peer halt. A disposable two-vCPU QEMU test injected re-entry at that point and observed the nested halt return one halted peer, followed by the timed reset and verified ext2 recovery. Since the failure preceded packet preparation, the journal remained unchanged. A nested panic after journal capture still retained the packet and reset successfully. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-early-nested-peerhalt-20261105/` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-nested-peerhalt-regression-20261105/`. Peer halt is best effort: an already-in-progress halt or an unresponsive CPU may leave a peer running. This is undeployed and not physical reset evidence.

The `KernelPanic` re-entrance guard now records its owning CPU. If that CPU enters panic again after recovery reset has been armed, the minimal nested handler attempts the existing delayed reset without rewriting the journal; a different CPU entering panic parks instead of resetting while the owner captures evidence. In disposable QEMU, a debugger re-entered `KernelPanic` on the owner immediately after journal capture: the armed case reset and the next recovery boot verified the original packet and repaired ext2; without the reset request the guest remained halted for seven seconds and the subsequent recovery boot retained the packet. A further QEMU test set an existing owner to the other vCPU and injected panic on the current CPU: it reached the park loop, did not reset over seven seconds, and did not modify the journal. This models the ownership state; it does not exercise two simultaneous real panics. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-nested-armed-20261105/`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-nested-unarmed-20261105/`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-peer-panic-20261105/`. Physical hardware is untested. A damaged stack, CPU identity or reset path may still prevent this fallback. The change is undeployed.

The armed panic journal is now attempted before the long serial hex dump, so a stall at that output cannot prevent the preceding capture. In disposable guarded-desktop QEMU, GDB stalled at the start of packet serial output; the already-written journal decoded to the injected panic, and a fresh recovery boot verified the packet and repaired ext2. The test stopped the stalled VM manually: it does not show automatic reset when the panic CPU itself stalls. A normal panic still emitted the same packet, waited, reset and recovered. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-serial-stall-20261105/` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-serial-order-regression-20261105/`. The disk attempt now precedes serial packet output, so an AHCI operation that itself never returns can instead delay that output; earlier raw serial diagnostics remain available. The change is undeployed.

`KernelPanic` now gathers process, system and bounded stack information for its structured packet even if the framebuffer is unavailable, matching the existing visual path. A disposable guarded-desktop QEMU test forced its framebuffer lookup to return null and verified the decoded journal packet contained the panic reason, processes, system data, stack, CPU state and log; the timed reset and following recovery boot retained the packet and repaired the data volume. The regular display-path panic/reset regression also passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-headless-panic-20261105/` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-headless-screen-regression-20261105/`. The headless condition and panic were debugger-injected; this does not establish physical capture or eliminate faults while collecting diagnostics. The change is undeployed.

The opt-in guarded desktop has now passed a real stalled-vCPU watchdog test on a disposable four-vCPU QEMU disk. GDB stopped timer interrupts on one CPU after desktop mounting; another CPU detected 30 stagnant checks, captured a decoded panic with the stalled CPU and log, and issued the delayed QEMU reset. A fresh recovery boot validated the same journal packet and repaired the dirty ext2 volume; offline checks passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-watchdog-stall-20261105-run2/`. This software watchdog needs a functioning CPU and scheduler, and the reset is a QEMU-only test path; neither an all-CPU hang nor Dell reset reliability is established.

The opt-in guarded desktop has now passed a disposable QEMU checked-shutdown and next-boot test through its normal debug bridge. A UID-1000 bridge job wrote and synced a service file; the shutdown request reached `ready`, reported a clean, non-uncertain final desktop state, and the offline ext2 superblock carried the clean marker. FAT/ext2 checks, guard records and journal passed independent inspection. A fresh QEMU process then booted the same disk through a snapshot, rechecked the guard and started the desktop service without altering the verified source disk. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-bridge-shutdown-reboot-20261105/`. The test stopped the guest after quiescence rather than committing a physical power transition; it does not establish real Dell service shutdown or physical cache durability.

The opt-in guarded desktop now changes its debug bridge from the restricted recovery policy to normal desktop capabilities only after the checked handoff and successful startup script, with shutdown admission still open. The transition is published atomically and the same boot-pinned session remains valid. In disposable QEMU with virtio networking, a test-only pause during handoff verified that power and command jobs were unavailable; after startup, the bridge reported both and a UID-1000 guest job completed. A second run deliberately failed the startup script and verified that the bridge remained restricted. Evidence is `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-bridge-20261105/bridge-transition.json` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-bridge-failed-script-20261105/bridge-transition.json`. The fixture's pause is confined to the QEMU-only reset-test build; this is not deployed or tested on the Dell, and broader lifecycle and real-application testing remain outstanding.

The guarded desktop now checks the flushed ext2 dirty marker by rereading and reclassifying the superblock before mounting; a failed or mismatched readback refuses handoff and is not retried. The shared direct-SATA normal boot also passed its disposable idle-flush and offline ext2 readback regression. A separate `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP_RESET_TEST` build option, off by default and rejected by the recovery-pair preparer, can arm the existing timed panic reset only when the disposable QEMU fixture explicitly requests both its reset test and Q35 power mode. A desktop panic then captured the journal, reset, and a fresh guarded boot retrieved the packet and repaired the dirty data volume (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-panic-reset-timed-20261105/`). The same test build stayed unarmed without the request (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-reset-unarmed-20261105/`). During orderly shutdown it disarms before final sync; an injected panic at final data sync remained halted for seven seconds and the subsequent recovery boot repaired the volume (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-shutdown-panic-20261105/`). These are QEMU-only tests, not physical durability or boot-path validation. Physical desktop panic reset is not enabled; firmware inventory and a reliable independent watchdog are still needed.

An opt-in `BROOK_SSD_GUARDED_DESKTOP` build now joins the automatic guard kernel to the previously QEMU-only checked desktop handoff. On a clean identity-bound data volume with matching clean guard records, it requires the checked private FAT mount and a pinned, validated panic journal, publishes that exact mount, retains the data reservation, arms journal capture, mounts the desktop and launches the startup script. It is off by default and requires `BROOK_SSD_AUTO_RECOVERY`; the existing recovery-pair preparer explicitly rejects it. In disposable QEMU, an automatic repair reset into this checked desktop and a UID-1000 service wrote and synced data (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-handoff-v3-20261105/`). A separate injected panic after desktop mount produced a verified journal packet; the halted VM was stopped and a fresh boot retrieved the packet, repaired the dirty data volume and reset (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-panic-recovery-v3-20261105/`). A cross-linked journal was refused without writes (`build/hardware/guard-auto-desktop-crosslink-20261105.log`). This is an experimental QEMU fixture, not a deployed normal boot: desktop panic reset remains unarmed, the debug bridge remains recovery-restricted, real Dell services and lifecycle concurrency are unverified, and firmware entrypoint inventory and safe activation are still required.

A disposable automatic-recovery test now deliberately makes a second FAT directory entry share the panic journal's first cluster. The pinned FAT checker reports the crosslink and exits nonzero; recovery does not pin or arm the journal, publish pending records or start ext2 repair, and the entire disposable disk remains byte-identical after the guest is stopped. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-crosslinked-journal-verified-20261105.log`. This verifies the checked recovery boundary, not normal-boot safety: a future normal panic writer must retain an equivalent clean-volume proof and journal lease before issuing raw sector writes.

The read-only PCH PCI diagnostic now separately samples PCI configuration DWORD 0xf0 (RCBA) twice with repeated exact-device identity checks. It reports the raw value only if stable; it does not map the window, read GCS, establish reset inhibition or authorize writes. [Linux's LPC resource definitions](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/mfd/lpc_ich.c) identify the RCBA configuration register and GCS offset, while its [TCO driver](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/watchdog/iTCO_wdt.c) identifies the version-2 GCS reset-inhibit bit. Host admission/bridge tests and normal/recovery builds pass. The matched, undeployed candidate `build/hardware/dell-pch-rcba-inventory-candidate-20261105/` also passed a disposable QEMU SATA/USB-network boot and foreign-PCH refusal, evidence `build/hardware/dell-pch-rcba-inventory-qemu-20261105/`. This remains untested on the Dell; boot-resource classification, UC mapping, firmware ownership and exact-register validation are still prerequisites for any physical MMIO observation.

The undeployed PCH watchdog status probe now also samples the 32-bit SMI enable register twice at ACPIBASE+0x30, after the exact PCH identity, decode and FADT timer cross-checks and before rechecking the PCI configuration. It rejects unstable or all-ones SMI reads and reports the raw value; it performs no watchdog or SMI writes. [Linux's LPC resource definitions](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/mfd/lpc_ich.c) identify the SMI offset, and its [TCO driver](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/watchdog/iTCO_wdt.c) identifies the TCO enable bit and separately checks reset inhibition. The host admission/bridge tests and normal and recovery kernel builds pass. The exact matched normal kernel/initrd candidate at `build/hardware/dell-pch-smi-inventory-candidate-20261105/` booted on disposable QEMU SATA with emulated USB networking, refused the foreign PCH probe and completed checked shutdown; evidence is `build/hardware/dell-pch-smi-inventory-qemu-20261105/`. It has not been staged, deployed or physically tested. This value has not been read from the Dell: its currently deployed build returns unknown command. Even a stable value cannot establish exclusive firmware/SMM ownership or safe watchdog arming.

Panic packets are now prepared and written to the already-armed journal before any panic-screen framebuffer drawing, QR encoding or display transfer. The renderer consumes that exact prepared packet rather than rebuilding it. A disposable QEMU test stalled immediately after preparation, before the background fill, and verified the captured packet on disk and on the subsequent recovery boot; a normal panic/recovery regression and a host prepared-QR rendering check also passed. The stall test intentionally stops the guest and does not show automatic reset from a wedged renderer. Packet construction and the earlier diagnostic collection can still fail, and the change is not deployed to the Dell. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-screen-stall-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`.

The automatic-recovery double-fault handler now asks peers to halt and attempts the already-armed timed reset after its minimal serial dump. It does not attempt a disk journal write in that fragile context. Disposable QEMU tests invalidated the #PF gate and triggered a page fault, producing a processor double fault; GDB confirmed entry on the dedicated IST stack. The armed case reset and completed the guarded retry, while the unarmed case remained halted for the observation interval. Serial, GDB and reboot logs use the prefixes `build/hardware/guard-auto-real-double-fault-verified-20261105` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-real-double-fault-unarmed-20261105`. The guest was deliberately modified to provoke the exception, and these tests do not prove peer halt or reset on physical hardware. The change is not deployed.

The automatic-recovery reserved-bit page-fault branch now invokes the already-armed panic reset after its serial diagnostics rather than always halting. It still deliberately avoids QR rendering and a disk-journal write because page tables may be corrupt. Its PMM history lookup now uses a nonblocking lock attempt, its raw history output has a bounded UART wait, and an armed reset skips the potentially unbounded reverse-map and corrupt-frame reads. A disposable QEMU test used GDB to classify a #UD frame as a supervisor reserved-bit page fault and inject a held PMM lock; it verified the busy-lock diagnostic, timed reset, untouched blank panic journal, and guarded repair on the following boot. Evidence is `build/hardware/guard-auto-rsvd-pmm-held-20261105.log` and its `.reboot.log`. This is undeployed; other earlier diagnostics can still fault or block, and the injection does not prove recovery from real page-table corruption.

The normal kernel watchdog warning now uses bounded emergency serial output, so a stalled CPU holding the ordinary serial ticket lock cannot block the monitoring CPU while it tries to report the stall. A disposable TCG/QEMU normal boot test injected a held serial ticket and a stagnant CPU sample with GDB, then observed the CPU1 warning; this is not a physical hang test. The automatic-recovery kernel also builds. This change is not deployed to the Dell. The watchdog still needs a running monitoring CPU and scheduler, and normal boot does not yet automatically reset on this warning.


The normal desktop launch environment now retains the virtio-specific Mesa GL override and Vulkan ICD only when the registered virtio app backend exists. Without it, those two overrides are absent so Mesa can choose an available driver; DRI/EGL paths and staged presentation remain. The yquake2 wrapper template no longer unconditionally replaces the inherited driver choice. Host environment/context tests pass; a disposable non-virtio SATA boot launched a UID-1000 process that verified the actual environment, and the normal panic-bridge regression also passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/gpu-env-nonvirtio-20261105/` and `build/hardware/gpu-env-panic-bridge-20261105/`. The wrapper generator was later located in `nix/experiment-packages.nix`; the updated wrapper has not been installed on the Dell. This removes a launcher obstacle but does not implement Intel DRM or prove Intel GL/Vulkan rendering; virtual GPU runtime rendering was not rerun for this change.

The current Dell boot's read-only `gpu-gop-plan` report confirms the previously configured BCS forcewake sample completed and released, with idle-looking samples and legacy submission mode. `gpu-vtd` reported its boot probe was not requested, so it provides no current translation-state observation. Neither result establishes GPU ownership or permits submission; no new GPU MMIO operation was initiated for these queries.

Prepared `build/hardware/dell-normal-panic-snapshot-candidate-20261105/` from the last confirmed Dell initrd lineage and the current normal kernel. The preparer verified the selected kernel hash, all ABI-65 modules, and pinned FAT checker and panic exporter readback; the already present ext2 checker remains in the initrd.
