The exact candidate pair passed a disposable KVM SATA boot with emulated xHCI USB networking, foreign-PCH watchdog refusal, bridge inspection and checked shutdown: `build/hardware/dell-normal-panic-snapshot-qemu-20261105/`. The normal-kernel panic snapshot was separately tested with an identity-matched QEMU data disk and real bridge retrieval. The Dell remains reachable on boot `70146d8ac9ff4467ad99969561842ade`, still running build `7fdd2838`; this candidate has not been staged, activated or physically tested. The firmware inventory request remains pending, and the QEMU test does not establish Dell USB or physical SSD behavior.

The combined disposable test now boots the ordinary (non-guard-test) kernel after a panic-interrupted repair. It captures the injected panic to the journal, observes the reset, resumes and verifies repair on attempt two, observes the next reset, then boots normal desktop and retrieves the identical packet through the real hardware debug bridge. The recovered packet decodes to the injected reason and includes the first-attempt recovery log; guard records, journal, GPT, service data and offline filesystem checks pass. Evidence: `build/hardware/panic-repair-normal-bridge-final-20261105/`, including the retrieved packet and decoded JSON. The resets were observed with QEMU `-no-reboot`, followed by new QEMU processes on the same disposable disk. This is not a physical power-loss or Dell reset test, nor does the current normal kernel automatically capture a new panic to disk.

Normal boot now takes a read-only, boot-lifetime snapshot of the newest CRC-validated `PANIC.BIN` record on the admitted system ESP before user processes start. It exposes the existing `bridge hardware recovery-panic` API and advertises that capability, allowing the existing `hw_recovery_panic` bridge workflow to retrieve it on a normal boot. The loader verifies the exact mounted-volume membership and fixed file size, retains no sector map and grants no panic-write authority. Host tests cover absent ownership, directory/size rejection, read failure, corrupt payload, one-shot loading and immutable snapshot; normal and recovery debug-command tests pass. Disposable QEMU direct-SATA boots accepted a valid record, rejected empty/corrupt records and left the journal unchanged. A normal boot with emulated virtio Ethernet retrieved the exact seeded packet using the real hardware bridge; serial evidence `build/hardware/normal-panic-snapshot-20261105/serial.log`. The normal and automatic-recovery kernels build. This has not been deployed to the Dell; it does not write panic records, authenticate journal contents, or prove physical storage durability.

The combined repair-to-desktop KVM test now also injects a panic after durable authorization of the first repair attempt. The panic journal packet matched serial byte-for-byte; after the timed reset, the next recovery boot reported the same packet length and CRC, consumed attempt two, verified ext2 and completed the guard. A subsequent boot selected the guarded desktop and ran the UID-1000 service, with the panic record preserved. The test also verifies no disk changes outside the ESP before retry, matching clean guards, unchanged GPT, service data and offline FAT/ext2 checks. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-panic-repair-desktop-final-20261105/`. It uses GDB fault injection, disposable QEMU disks and a fresh QEMU process after each observed reset; it does not establish physical crash capture, firmware reset or production guarded startup.

An end-to-end disposable KVM disk now combines the automatic-repair recovery pair with the test-only guarded desktop pair. Without F5, firmware detected the dirty ext2 state, selected recovery, completed and verified repair, published matching clean guards, and issued a reset. The harness observed the QEMU reset, independently checked the repaired disk, and launched the next QEMU boot on that same disk; firmware selected the guarded desktop image, which checked the ESP, retained the journal, prepared home and ran a UID-1000 service. The journal, clean guard records and GPT remained intact, and offline FAT/ext2 checks and service-data readback passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-repair-desktop-final-20261105/`; reproducible harness: `scripts/test_guard_repair_handoff_qemu.py`. Its compact initrds and both disk identities are QEMU-only. The second boot is a fresh QEMU process after observing reset, and this does not prove a production normal kernel, physical durability, Dell reset behavior, or firmware entrypoint safety.

The QEMU-only post-check startup experiment now reruns the existing desktop-home preparation after the guarded data mount, before the startup script. Disposable KVM tests cover both a fresh home and an existing settings file: directories have UID/GID 1000, defaults are installed only when absent, existing settings survive, and a UID-1000 service writes and syncs successfully. Independent filesystem checks passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-home-final-journal-desktop-script-20261105/` and `build/hardware/guard-home-final-journal-desktop-script-preserve-20261105/`. The deferred call is restricted to the test selector; guarded production startup and live Dell services remain unverified.

In a disposable QEMU-only guarded handoff, the checker worker now has a test selector that runs an init script after the scheduler starts. The fixture script uses the normal Dell script's window-manager, framebuffer, scheduler and console commands and launches a synthetic UID-1000 service; that service verifies its UID, writes and fsyncs its home file, and the harness verifies the file and checks both filesystems offline. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-desktop-service-final-qemu-20261105/`. This confirms this limited startup sequence and service I/O work after guarded publication; the deliberately minimal app tree caused launcher warnings, the real Dell services and home preparation were not tested, and calling the script after scheduler startup still needs concurrency/lifecycle review. It is test-only, not an automatic production boot path, and nothing was deployed to the Dell.

The QEMU-only guarded desktop handoff can now publish the checked FAT mount's exact VFS publication identity to the existing system-volume ownership checks, after validating the retained mount root and reserved device. A forged publication is rejected and consumes the test-only adoption attempt; unrelated files do not pass the ownership check. The change also permits a legacy FAT root open when a journal file is pinned, without permitting access to the leased journal. Disposable KVM tests passed identity refusal, failed desktop publication, checked shutdown and next boot, panic capture/reset, and journal mutation protection; evidence under `build/hardware/guard-identity-root-final-*` and `guard-identity-root-journal-20261105/`. Host VFS and FAT tests passed and the automatic-recovery kernel builds. The system-volume adoption remains guarded by `BROOK_SSD_GUARD_PENDING_TEST`, and these tests do not demonstrate actual update-tool execution or a production normal boot. No Dell files were changed.

The guarded handoff's checked-shutdown test exposed a headless lifecycle stall: close polling ran only in the window-manager render loop, so shutdown remained in `closing` without that scene. The compositor thread now polls shutdown outside the rendering branch. In a disposable KVM fixture, the real shutdown coordinator drained, synced and reached `ready` with the checked ESP, pinned journal and guarded ext2 lease still held; the ext2 clean flag, witness, unchanged journal and guards, GPT, and independent FAT/ext2 checks were verified, then another boot successfully handed off the same volume. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-desktop-shutdown-reboot-qemu-20261105/`. Existing shutdown coordinator host tests and the automatic-recovery kernel build passed. This does not establish physical power-loss durability or prove shutdown with a halted compositor or live GUI applications. The guarded desktop handoff is still test-only and has not been deployed.

The guarded handoff exposed a legacy VFS lookup mismatch: FAT reported the retained mountpoint as `/MEDIA/SYSTEM`, while old kernel callers used `/media/system`. Legacy lookup now considers an ASCII-case variant only after a retained walk proves that the actual filesystem lookup reaches the same mounted object; it does not make a case-sensitive backing case-insensitive. The host VFS suite checks the case-sensitive refusal. Disposable KVM tests now read the EFI loader through the legacy lowercase path after guarded publication and pass both desktop handoff and panic/reset/journal re-pin; evidence `build/hardware/guard-legacy-final-journal-desktop-20261105/` and `build/hardware/guard-legacy-final-journal-desktop-panic-20261105/`. The automatic-recovery kernel builds. The change has not been deployed to the Dell, and non-ASCII aliases are not established by these tests.

A QEMU-only guarded desktop handoff prototype now retains the identity-bound disk reservation and pinned panic journal while mounting a clean ext2 desktop volume. Disposable KVM tests verified a synced desktop witness, refusal of a dirty volume without disk changes, denial of a write through an adapter after desktop publication failed, and a panic packet captured to the journal followed by reset and successful re-pinning on the next boot. Offline FAT and ext2 checks and GPT/guard preservation checks passed. Evidence is in `build/hardware/guard-final-journal-desktop-20261105/`, `guard-final-journal-desktop-dirty-20261105/`, `guard-final-journal-desktop-panic-20261105/`, and `guard-desktop-failed-qemu-20261105/`. This path is enabled only by `BROOK_SSD_GUARD_PENDING_TEST`; its fixture pair is QEMU-only and must not be deployed. It does not yet prove a normal production desktop boot, post-repair handoff, physical panic durability, or concurrent lifecycle safety. The existing Dell boot and loader remain unchanged.

The Dell diagnostic normal-boot pair `build/hardware/dell-pch-inspect-candidate-20261105/` was built from the current normal kernel and the last confirmed Dell initrd with matching ABI-65 modules. Its exact pair passed a disposable KVM SATA/USB-network boot; its kernel also passed a direct-SATA idle-writeback and offline ext2 check on a private fixture. The Dell updater staged the pair in RAM, then a separate authorized transaction activated generation 25, slot 0, and requested a checked restart. Receipt: `build/hardware/dell-pch-inspect-activate-20261105/receipt.json`, transaction `1e1a447d250d477fbce11800875c09d6`, power request `fcd4dafb46484f7eb040d909bcb222f6`. The 180-second boot verification expired without a new identity, and doctor then reported `No route to host`. Ian subsequently reported the Dell had remained locally responsive and power-cycled it; the current boot `70146d8ac9ff4467ad99969561842ade`, session `208b0ab378694451b0a1e1e95d7f1b94`, reports kernel `7fdd2838`, the expected `dell-pch-inspect-20261105` payload and a ready writable desktop. The earlier timed-out receipt remains historical and must not be replayed. A boot-pinned readback job `1600f778012d4853889815467c3f361c` confirmed both original EFI loader hashes, the staged inventory EFI hash, equal guard-file hashes, and the original blank panic-journal hash; it does not establish power-loss durability. The current firmware inventory contains 27 entries; 13 allowed entries were readable and none was WDAT, while 14 entries were unavailable through the restricted API, so absence is not proven. The live PCH configuration command reported stable boot and live DWORDs `0x40=0x1801`, `0x44=0x80`; no TCO register was accessed. The existing default loader still does not enforce the recovery guard. The USB-link failure mechanism remains unconfirmed.

The checksum-validated ACPI debug inventory now permits read-only copying of WDAT watchdog description tables in addition to its existing AML and DMAR allowlist. This is preparatory evidence for an independent hardware watchdog, which could reset a completely stalled system; it does not interpret or execute WDAT instructions or touch watchdog registers. The existing ACPI reader host fixture covers WDAT access, checksum failure and continued rejection of MSDM, and the automatic recovery kernel builds. This is not deployed to the Dell, so the Dell's current WDAT availability and its watchdog behavior remain unknown. The earlier private capture `build/hardware/dell-acpi-capture-20261031/manifest.json` has 26 hash-verified retained tables and no WDAT among them; one sensitive table was withheld, so this is not a complete current inventory. The previously observed Intel `8086:9cc3` PCH is mapped to Wildcat Point LP by the [Linux LPC driver](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/mfd/lpc_ich.c), making chipset TCO another possible path. The [Linux iTCO driver](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/watchdog/iTCO_wdt.c) checks reset inhibition and SMI ownership before operation; the historical FADT timer address alone does not establish TCO decode, ownership or permission to write those registers. The [Linux WDAT driver](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/drivers/watchdog/wdat_wdt.c) similarly illustrates why firmware-specified actions and resource ownership must be audited before enabling a watchdog.

The same historical Dell DSDT disassembly identifies `PMBA` as `0x1800`, consistent with its FADT PM timer at `0x1808`. The [Intel 9-series register reference](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/datasheets/9-series-chipset-pch-datasheet.pdf) describes TCO I/O relative to a PM base; this suggests where to investigate, but is not proof of this particular live chipset's decode or safe ownership. The next hardware-watchdog step is an explicitly read-only, boot-bound inventory of the exact chipset's PCI decode and watchdog status, cross-checked with its applicable LP documentation; do not arm it on the basis of the historical table or a calculated port alone.

The PCI boot inventory now snapshots raw configuration DWORDs `0x40` and `0x44` only for Intel `8086:9cc3` at `00:1f.0`, and exposes them in the existing read-only PCI inventory response. This is boot-time configuration access, not a runtime arbitrary-address API; it does not access TCO I/O ports or interpret the fields as permission to touch them. Host tests cover exact BDF and identity admission, no reads on mismatch, and debug response serialization. The running Dell's boot-pinned PCI inventory on `b53fff60c2c34b26ab517bf62dcf5d8e` confirms that exact LPC identity and location, but the existing build does not include these new fields. The recovery kernel builds, but this addition is not on the Dell and the actual watchdog status is not yet inventoried.

PCI configuration mechanism 1 now serializes each shared CF8/CFC address/data pair with an IRQ-safe lock. A 16-bit write uses a 16-bit data-port operation rather than reading and rewriting its neighboring half, which avoids clearing adjacent write-one-to-clear status bits. A concurrent host test exercises interleaved reads and the exact write widths, and the changed recovery kernel booted, repaired and restarted on a disposable KVM disk; evidence `build/hardware/guard-auto-pci-serialized-normal-20261105.log`. Higher-level read/modify/write sequences are not made atomic by this change, and the running Dell retains the previous unsynchronized implementation. No live PCI watchdog probe is enabled by this change.

The normal debug bridge now also has a read-only `bridge hardware pch-watchdog-pci` command: it requires a complete boot inventory containing exactly one captured `8086:9cc3` at `00:1f.0`, rechecks the PCI identity and both raw configuration DWORDs twice, and reports boot and live values only if both observations agree. Host tests cover missing identity, failed/unstable reads and response encoding; the recovery build compiles but its restricted listener does not permit this command. It reads no TCO port or watchdog status, and has not been deployed or exercised on the Dell. PCI configuration access must use the serialized kernel implementation described above; consistency of two samples is not proof firmware cannot change the configuration afterward.

A separate normal-boot `bridge hardware pch-watchdog-status` candidate adds three 16-bit read-only TCO observations (control, timeout status and initial timer). It requires the same complete exact-device inventory and stable PCI identity/configuration, validates the enabled ACPI decode and cross-checks PMBASE against the validated FADT PM timer port, then rechecks PCI configuration after the reads. Host tests cover admission failures before any port access, changed configuration, raw output and restricted recovery listener; the normal kernel builds. No watchdog state is modified, no ownership is claimed, and firmware/SMM can still change decode during the observation. This command is not in the currently running Dell build and has not been exercised on hardware. Its offsets follow the [Intel TCO register reference](https://www.intel.com/content/dam/www/public/us/en/documents/datasheets/9-series-chipset-pch-datasheet.pdf) and the [FreeBSD Wildcat Point-LP watchdog driver](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/main/sys/dev/ichwd/ichwd.c); chipset-specific behavior still requires physical validation before arming a watchdog.

The matched normal-boot pair `build/hardware/dell-pch-status-candidate-20261105/` uses the current Dell initrd policy and ABI-65 modules. Its exact files passed the disposable KVM SATA/USB-network boot and the watchdog command refused the foreign QEMU chipset; evidence `build/hardware/dell-pch-status-qemu-20261105/`. It is not activated or physically tested. The current firmware inventory request is pending; do not interrupt Ian's firmware selection with a remote restart. The inactive-slot updater has no automatic rollback for a valid kernel that hangs.

The normal kernel/initrd pair preparer now optionally embeds the same pinned `FATFSCK.ELF` used by recovery, in addition to its existing `PANICLOG.ELF` option. The current Dell initrd already contains the matching pinned `E2FSCK.ELF`. `build/hardware/dell-recovery-tools-candidate-20261105/` contains all three; the preparer validates static ELF inputs, checks the FAT checker pin and reads both added files back. Its eight host tests passed and this exact candidate booted in disposable KVM with foreign-watchdog refusal; evidence `build/hardware/dell-recovery-tools-qemu-20261105/`. This pair is not deployed. Copying these utilities into normal boot does not provide a writable checker device, automatic repair, or a normal-boot panic writer, and the firmware inventory remains pending.

The automatic-recovery watchdog warning now uses bounded emergency serial output rather than waiting on the ordinary serial ticket lock. In disposable KVM, GDB left the serial lock held and stalled a vCPU with interrupts disabled; the warning still appeared, another CPU captured the watchdog panic after the full interval, the machine reset, and the bounded second repair completed with an independent ext2 check. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-held-serial-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`; `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-serial-pair-20261105/` is QEMU-only. Other code can still block on that lock, and this does not establish recovery if the entire scheduler stalls or on the physical Dell.

The isolated automatic-recovery kernel now escalates a previously progressing peer CPU whose timer accounting is unchanged for 30 watchdog samples, but only after the durable repair gate has armed panic reset. It captures the panic using the existing journal path and then follows the existing delayed reset. It deliberately ignores stalls predating authorization or CPUs never seen to progress. Host policy tests covered the 30-sample threshold and re-arming; a disposable KVM debugger test held the repair worker and injected the final stalled sample, then verified the watchdog reason in the panic packet, disk capture, timed reset, second repair attempt and independent ext2 verification. A further KVM test supplied a constant simulated sample for the full interval, and another disabled interrupts on the actual repair vCPU and placed it in a loop: after the full interval, another CPU detected the stalled vCPU, captured the packet, reset and completed the second attempt. The hard-stall test primes the watchdog observation baseline through GDB, then detaches; it does not emulate all possible hardware failures. Ordinary repair still passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-injected-v2-20261105.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-duration-20261105.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-hard-stall-20261105.log` and its `.reboot.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-watchdog-normal-20261105.log`. The `guard-auto-watchdog-pair-20261105/` payload is QEMU-only. Ordinary boot hangs, total scheduler lockup, and physical firmware reset remain unverified. This software watchdog depends on a working scheduler and cannot detect a system-wide hard lockup.

The automatic recovery worker now reads the previously captured panic from the checked ESP before refusing an invalid or unsupported data-filesystem superblock, or an unreadable guard pair. It still performs no attempt or repair after either refusal; arming the panic writer and publishing the test mount continue to require successful guard inspection. Disposable KVM tests captured a panic after pending authorization, then separately (1) changed the data superblock to an unsupported feature set while preserving its identity and (2) removed one guard file. Each recovery boot retrieved the identical packet over emulated USB Ethernet and left the complete disk hash unchanged. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-invalid-diagnostics-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-missing-diagnostics-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`. Their `guard-auto-*-diagnostics-pair-20261105/` directories are ad hoc QEMU-only test pairs, never Dell payloads. The ESP must still pass its independent FAT check, and the disk and filesystem identities must pass admission before this path can retrieve the packet.

The undeployed automatic-recovery candidate now permits at most two durable repair attempts for a matching, identity-bound pending guard pair. Each attempt is recorded and read back before repair writes or the panic reset are enabled; mismatched, invalid, or exhausted records remain in maintenance, as does any transaction whose completion is uncertain during that boot. On a later boot a matching, independently checked pair can be reconsidered. A resumed attempt checks and verifies ext2 even if its superblock appears clean, then clears the counter only as part of verified guard completion. Existing EFI builds treat a nonzero counter as invalid and therefore continue to block normal boot. An interrupted KVM repair captured a panic, automatically reset, exposed the preserved packet over emulated USB Ethernet during a bounded retrieval window, consumed the second attempt, verified ext2 and completed the guard; a separate exhausted fixture made no disk writes. Offline FAT and ext2 checks passed, as did an ordinary repair and host guard fault tests. A clean-ext2 pending-pair fixture also consumed attempt two, completed the guard, passed independent offline ext2 verification and rebooted normally with the rebuilt EFI. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-retry-offline-20261105.log` and its `.reboot.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-retry-exhausted-final-20261105.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-retry-normal-20261105.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-pending-clean-20261105.log`. The pair `build/hardware/guard-auto-retry-usb-pair-20261105/` is QEMU-only. The previously prepared Dell candidate predates this change and has not been deployed; firmware entrypoint inventory and a safe loader migration remain prerequisites to physical activation. The Dell's keyboard and touchpad failure remains unexplained.

The retained FAT backend now supports child removal and rename to an absent name through exact retained parents. It refuses a target with another retained reference or an open FIL, including the crash journal's fixed lease; nonempty directories return `ENOTEMPTY` and directory moves reject cycles. Replacing a different existing target returns `EOPNOTSUPP`, rather than claiming an atomic replacement that this FAT implementation cannot provide. As with upstream FAT rename, a power failure during a move can require filesystem checking. Host FAT adapter/backend tests pass. In the QEMU-only checked-publication fixture, removal or rename of the journal, replacement of the journal, and removal or rename of an ordinary open file returned `EBUSY`; removal and rename after close succeeded. The existing journal bytes and disk outside the ESP were unchanged and `fsck.fat -n` passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-journal-rename-qemu-20261105/`; the paired kernel under `build/hardware/guard-journal-rename-pair-20261105/` is test-only and must not be deployed. The private-to-production mount handoff and physical panic writer remain unfinished.

The QEMU-only checked-publication path can now hand its pinned sector map to the existing panic-safe AHCI writer, only with a separate explicit test selector and the exact admitted KVM fixture. The integrated KVM test checked and published the reserved FAT mount, forced a headless panic, captured a packet identical to serial in journal sequence 8 while preserving the existing sequence-7 record, confirmed the timed Q35 reset, and booted the disk again to recheck and pin the captured journal. Offline FAT checking passed and writes outside the ESP were absent. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-journal-panic-qemu-final-v2-20261105/`; `build/hardware/guard-journal-panic-pair-20261105/` is a test-only payload and must never be deployed. This does not establish physical-device durability, production handoff, or normal-boot automatic recovery.

Publication now records attempted and successful handoff separately: a failed mount cannot arm the panic writer or be retried. Disposable KVM cases verified arming before publication is rejected, failed publication stays unarmed, the test selector is required, and successful capture/reset/reboot still works. The tested Q35 firmware selected its ACPI I/O reset register (`power: reset=acpi-io8`); this does not prove the Dell's firmware reset or timeout behavior. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-arm-final-journal-publish-panic-20261105/`, `build/hardware/guard-arm-final-journal-publish-unarmed-20261105/`, and `build/hardware/guard-arm-final-journal-publish-failed-20261105/`. Their paired image is test-only.

The isolated `BROOK_SSD_AUTO_RECOVERY` candidate now attempts to pin the checked journal and arm the AHCI panic writer after guarded write authorization and before the pending repair transaction. In a disposable KVM automatic-repair fixture it reported `pin=0 arm=0`, repaired and verified the dirty ext2 volume, completed the guard transaction, reset and reached normal boot. With the journal absent it reported `pin=-2 arm=-2` and still completed repair. A separate GDB-injected panic at the pending transaction entry produced a disk packet matching serial, including the injected reason and recent log; only journal sectors changed, offline FAT checking passed, the Q35 test reset fired, and the next boot checked and pinned the record again. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-arm-20261105.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-absent-20261105.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-injected-final-v3-20261105.log` with its `.reboot.log`; the fixture pair is `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-pair-fixture-20261105/`.

The automatic-recovery candidate separately arms a five-second firmware panic reset only after both pending records have been durably verified. A GDB-injected panic after that point captured the journal, waited at least four seconds, reset through QEMU's ACPI reset register, and booted into guarded maintenance with both pending records intact. A pre-pending panic remained unarmed for seven seconds, and an ordinary repair still completed and rebooted. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-reset-final-20261105.log` and its `.reboot.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-panic-reset-unarmed-v2-20261105.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-reset-normal-20261105.log`; the QEMU fixture pair is `build/hardware/guard-auto-reset-pair-fixture-20261105/`.

If the panic PIT delay fails, the candidate falls back to a validated FADT System-I/O ACPI power-management timer, using bounded 50 ms intervals and its low 24 bits to handle wrap. Once capture has been attempted and recovery has explicitly armed reset, failure of both timer paths (or lack of a supported PM timer) now causes a last-resort reset attempt without the intended display delay. A disposable QEMU test forced both timer helpers to return failure through GDB; it verified journal capture, the timerless reset attempt, and guarded repair on the following boot. A separate run forced only the PIT failure and verified the PM-timer delay of at least four seconds, reset and recovery. Serial evidence is `build/hardware/guard-auto-timerless-final-20261105.log` and `build/hardware/guard-auto-pmtimer-regression-final-20261105.log`; the private fixture pair is `build/hardware/guard-auto-timerless-pair-fixture-20261105/`. These are simulated timer failures, not physical failure or power-loss tests. The change is undeployed, does not cover ordinary boot or all hangs, and does not resolve Dell firmware entrypoint inventory or establish physical reset and crash-write durability.

The automatic recovery worker now pins and validates the previous journal before rejecting pending guard records, and keeps the newest verified packet in immutable boot memory. A bounded `bridge hardware recovery-panic <offset> <count>` command exposes its metadata and up to 512 bytes per call; host tests cover missing records, ranges and encoding. In disposable KVM, an injected panic after pending state reset into maintenance, where the reported sequence, length and CRC matched the captured packet before the pending guard stopped repair. Normal repair and a clean-disk check also passed. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-prior-panic-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`, `build/hardware/guard-auto-prior-normal-20261105.log`, and `build/hardware/guard-auto-prior-clean-20261105.log`; the fixture pair is `build/hardware/guard-auto-prior-pair-fixture-20261105/`.

The automatic recovery candidate now starts a restricted debug listener when a network interface is present. It allows boot identity, capabilities, logs and the retained panic packet, while refusing job, power and other commands. `hw_recovery_panic` reads the snapshot over the boot-pinned bridge, checks chunk metadata and CRC, and creates a new local packet file. A disposable virtio-net KVM test captured a panic, reset into pending maintenance, retrieved the identical packet through the hardware bridge, and confirmed a power command was rejected. The image preparer can optionally include the matching build's `virtio_net` module for a QEMU fixture or `xhci` for physical recovery, with an explicit ABI check and manifest hash. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-debug-network-final-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`; `build/hardware/guard-auto-debug-pair-final-20261105/` is QEMU-only and must not be deployed. This does not prove the Dell's USB network or physical reset works in guarded recovery. Reload the MCP client to discover the new tool after installing updated bridge source.

The same panic/reset/remote-retrieval test also passed on disposable KVM using an emulated xHCI USB CDC-ECM adapter and the recovery build's `xhci` module. It confirmed the retained packet and the restricted listener's power-command refusal. Evidence: `build/hardware/guard-auto-usb-network-20261105.log` and `.reboot.log`, with QEMU-only pair `build/hardware/guard-auto-usb-pair-fixture-20261105/`. The Dell remained reachable on boot `b53fff60c2c34b26ab517bf62dcf5d8e`; its current debug image does not expose FADT bytes. An earlier Dell FADT capture at `build/hardware/dell-acpi-capture-20261031/001-FACP.aml` describes a 24-bit System-I/O PM timer at `0x1808`, and the host parser test covers that layout. This is historical firmware evidence, not a current-boot or physical timer/reset test.

A new physical-profile automatic recovery pair with the built xHCI module was prepared locally at `build/hardware/dell-auto-usb-debug-candidate-20261105/` using boot-pinned controller and disk observations from `b53fff60c2c34b26ab517bf62dcf5d8e` and the previously captured identity-bound ESP/data selectors. The preparer checked the kernel with `tools/update_elf_check.cpp`, the pinned checker hashes, and the network module ABI and SHA-256. The exact physical pair refused a foreign disposable KVM disk before recovery access and left the disk unchanged; serial evidence is `build/hardware/dell-auto-usb-debug-foreign-20261105.log`. The pair has not been installed, staged on the Dell, or booted physically. The selectors were not independently re-read in this step. Firmware entrypoint inventory and a safe activation/migration remain necessary before replacing any installed recovery or loader path.

Ian authorized unattended work on the Dell tonight: prioritize reliable recovery after failures and collecting failure evidence, then implement physical Intel HD accelerated 3D and prove it using existing yquake2 GL and Vulkan tests. If the Dell is offline and blocks further useful work, pause for Ian to reboot it. The former chat remains paused.

Ian expanded the recovery goal: make the recovery tooling available in the normal boot, automate recovery wherever feasible, enlarge boot text without undue complexity, and add timed hang/panic recovery. Capture panic details through the bridge where feasible and in a preallocated disk area that does not require filesystem metadata changes at failure time. Keep the separate recovery and USB paths as fallbacks. This request supersedes the earlier opt-in-only watchdog direction as a product goal; its safe arming, inhibition and loop prevention still need a design appropriate to automatic operation. A fully wedged kernel cannot be guaranteed to run a software handler.

The kernel console now selects the already-baked larger atlas for displays at least 2560×1440, and sizes its status region from that font. A disposable KVM boot at the Dell's 3200×1800 resolution reached the desktop and reported a 37-pixel line height rather than 19 pixels. The change has not been deployed to the Dell and does not enlarge firmware/UEFI loader text.

Physical results: Ian created a persistent firmware entry for BROOKF5.EFI and selected F5. Recovery boot `cb5b56e1a4e04858bd7c280c8af2d045` advertised build b4210c41 with the writable desktop disabled; its automatic read-only SSD check completed cleanly. Both diagnostic shortcuts appeared in the launcher catalog. Remote NETCHECK completed with exit 0 and a framed local bridge reply. Ian reported keyboard and touchpad unresponsive on this recovery boot, so local launcher interaction remains unverified. Earlier both inputs worked again after checked shutdown and a full power pull. The pre-F5 normal boot had reached the desktop; independent original-default and USB fallback checks remain to be assessed.

Current implementation progress: KernelPanic now emits the structured serial panic packet without a framebuffer, and the serial staging buffer accommodates its header. Host regression decodes the headless packet and kernel objects compile. This is not deployed or boot-tested, now also preserves structured serial output in the tested framebuffer exception path; it does not implement disk capture or panic network transport. The QEMU-only reset experiment is described below.

The structured packet now also includes up to 511 bytes of the panic reason, which previously existed only in the screen and ordinary serial text and could be lost from a journal snapshot. The decoder presents the reason in JSON or terminal-safe escaped text. The headless host test checks the bound and journal round-trip; disposable QEMU boots decoded the expected reason for deliberate panic, unarmed control, exception and reset followed by a second boot. The updated kernel is not deployed to the Dell, and the journal writer remains test-only.

The packet also includes up to 1024 bytes of the newest complete kernel log lines. Panic capture uses a nonblocking ring-lock attempt and records an unavailable status if another halted CPU holds the lock; it does not wait or attempt an unsafe lockless read. Host tests cover wraparound, bounded selection and lock contention. Disposable QEMU panic, unarmed, exception and reboot cases decoded the expected reason and an available recent boot log. This is not deployed to the Dell and does not establish physical journal or network delivery.

Crash decoder warnings now go to stderr so the optical receiver's JSON remains parseable. Dirty build IDs use the actual `<commit>+<digest>` format; for dirty or unmatched builds the decoder no longer guesses a current ELF and instead requires an explicitly supplied matching `--elf`. A clean archive is selected only by commit, with a warning that build options can still differ. Optical reports reserve unique names, including an exclusive raw-record create, so concurrent or closely spaced captures do not overwrite earlier reports. Host checks cover collision and dirty-ID handling; the disposable QEMU panic/reboot checks parse the decoder output directly as JSON.

Kernel panic and exception serial output now bypasses the ordinary ticket lock and abandons emergency UART output after one bounded readiness timeout. This avoids repeatedly waiting on a stuck UART or on a serial lock held by a halted or interrupted CPU before capture/reset. The timeout is a poll count rather than a calibrated time, and raw output can interleave before other CPUs halt. A host fake-UART test covers timeout and suppression; disposable QEMU panic, unarmed, exception and reset/reboot tests still produced decodable records. This is not yet deployed or tested with a physically stalled UART.

The disposable QEMU reset fixture now also deliberately panics while the panicking CPU holds the ordinary serial ticket lock. It emitted a decodable panic reason and log tail, waited for the test delay, and reached a second boot. The shell trigger is gated on the QEMU-only reset opt-in; an unarmed disposable boot rejected it. This proves the held-lock scenario on that VM path, not physical reset or a stalled UART.

The full exception handler now emits a structured packet even when no framebuffer is available. Its headless fallback records the exception, registers, build identity, per-CPU snapshot and log tail without walking the potentially damaged exception stack. An explicitly QEMU-only switch exercised that branch with #UD: the decoded packet contained the vector, RIP, build identity and log, and the VM reached a second boot. This is not deployed to the Dell; it does not establish that all exception classes can safely reach the packet builder.

Panic and exception stack walks and raw stack dumps are now constrained to the current process's bounded kernel-stack range; missing or implausible bounds omit that optional data. A QEMU-only #UD fixture set RBP to an invalid kernel-half address and still produced the original bad register value in a crash packet and reached a second boot. Host tests cover edge and overflow arithmetic. The range check does not establish that damaged page tables or corrupt process metadata are safe, and bootstrap/alternate stacks may yield shorter traces.

FAT crash-file mapping: a retained fixed-file lease can snapshot all 258 journal sectors with bounded extent, geometry, range and duplicate checks. Host FAT16, FAT32 and offset-volume fixtures used a deliberately fragmented file, exercised the journal through its map, checked no sectors outside it changed and passed offline fsck. The map remains diagnostic and is not authority for panic writes: third-file crosslinks and exclusive ownership across checking/mounting are not yet established.

Ian requested prompt idle-time durability. The former ext2 code batched metadata by operation count and started its background worker only when optional write-behind was enabled. The new default worker performs a five-second safety pass for pending metadata and unflushed backing writes; clean idle mounts are skipped. Failed flushes retain dirty state and errors; worker-start failure selects a synchronous fallback. Host ext2 tests cover low-volume metadata, direct writes, retries, fallback and queue age. Disposable TCG tests on both virtio ext2 and the identity-bound direct SATA path wrote without guest fsync, observed pending work clear after background sync, killed QEMU, and passed independent e2fsck/readback. Process termination is not a physical power cut or proof of SSD controller durability. The Dell has not received this build. The deliberate active-session dirty marker remains set until checked shutdown, so automatic dirty-store recovery is still needed.

Ordinary FAT mounts now also participate in the existing five-second file-writeback worker: buffered file writes and open-file creation mark the mount for a checked file and device sync; errors retain the pending state for retry, while clean or read-only mounts are skipped. Private recovery mounts remain outside this worker. Host FAT16/FAT32 and offset-volume tests exercised idle sync with the writer still open, failed flush and retry, empty-file creation, and mount removal. A disposable QEMU panic-journal boot still passed, but that boot was not a timed idle-flush test. This is not deployed to the Dell and is not a physical power-loss guarantee.

FAT-backed panic capture test: the disposable AHCI test kernel can pin a fixed FAT file on its verified synthetic system partition, snapshot its sectors and write the journal directly through the panic-safe AHCI gate. TCG/OVMF tests captured twice, verified alternating records against serial, used an independent FAT chain map to reject writes outside the file, and passed offline fsck; a short file was rejected. A deliberately fragmented chain also passed the full capture and fsck. This is test-only: the retained lease does not establish absence of crosslinks to other files, exclusive ownership through an offline check, physical SSD durability, or permission to enable this writer on the Dell.

`PANICLOG.ELF` exports the newest valid fixed-file journal packet to a new file without changing the journal; the desktop preparer builds it and the matched-pair preparer accepts it with `--panic-exporter`. For a journal available to ordinary VFS access, run `/boot/PANICLOG.ELF /media/system/PANIC.BIN /tmp/panic-packet.bin` through a guest job, transfer that RAM file through the bridge, and decode it on the host with `tools/crash_decoder.py --packet <file> --elf <matching-kernel>`. A disposable panic fixture captured twice and a subsequent regular kernel boot exported the newer packet with matching length and CRC; host tests covered damaged, ambiguous and truncated records and output collision. The existing panic writer is still test-only, so this does not imply a physical crash journal exists on the Dell.

The bridge source now provides `hw_panic_report`, a boot-pinned post-reboot export and authenticated download with durable export/transfer IDs and host length/CRC verification. Its `PANICLOG.ELF --bridge <artifact-id>` mode creates a new transfer artifact without overwriting another file. A disposable SATA panic fixture captured twice, booted a regular kernel and successfully ran both exporter modes with the expected sequence, length and CRC; offline FAT check passed. Host workflow tests cover stale boot, mismatched download and no automatic replay, and MCP registration was checked. This is not yet installed on the Dell or tested end-to-end over its live bridge; the physical journal and panic-time network delivery remain unimplemented.

The hardware bridge method was subsequently exercised end to end against a disposable KVM guest: it exported a valid seeded journal through a boot-pinned debug job and authenticated forwarded bulk connection, and the host packet, sequence, size and SHA-256 matched independently generated data. This validates the retrieval path on a VM; at that point the Dell had not received the new exporter or a physical panic journal.

Update: the Dell now has a newly allocated blank `/media/system/PANIC.BIN`, 258 sectors (132,096 bytes), created by physical job `9bad84b836994297adf6661acf92cca5` after the configured disk/partition identity and admitted system ESP were checked. The helper synced and reopened the file; independent job `658663e7ad0d4dbdacbd55713fb8292b` reported SHA-256 `8675651898d77ef1cbe478e28b4ef7e367fabcdd4e667f536d1a1a0ab6b7c2f2`, matching the all-zero file, and both original EFI loader hashes were unchanged. Preflight established the name was absent. The provisioner was exercised on a disposable Brook SATA disk with offline zero readback and FAT check. Evidence and IDs are under `build/hardware/dell-panic-journal-provision-20261105/`. The physical panic writer remains disabled: file-sector exclusivity, FAT crosslink exclusion and physical power-loss durability are not established.

An adversarial disposable KVM fixture now crosslinks a preallocated `PANIC.BIN` with another FAT file, then enters the reserved-volume recovery checker. The checker explicitly identified the two files sharing clusters, exited nonzero, did not reach guard-record admission and left the full disk hash unchanged. This confirms rejection in the reserved recovery path, not on the live Dell; a continuous reservation and checked handoff to the ordinary mount and pinned journal remain necessary before panic writes can be enabled.

An explicit disposable KVM-only path now consumes the tracked clean checker result, retains the original disk reservation, opens a geometry-matched private FAT mount and pins the preallocated journal without authorizing writes. It validates the journal sector map and record headers, and confirms that reopen, unlink and rename are refused while pinned; the mount and leases remain retained through the boot. Separate fixtures passed for a blank journal and a prior valid record, rejected short or corrupt journals, and rejected a crosslink before mounting; each disk hash remained unchanged. The original normal desktop mount is not published by this path, and no panic writer is enabled. Test-only payload: `build/hardware/guard-journal-pin-pair-v2-20261105/`; never deploy it to physical hardware.

The initial disposable publication experiment mounted the pinned private FAT instance and enabled ordinary writes. At that stage retained-path journal reopen returned `-EBUSY`, but unlink and rename were unsupported; those operations and the integrated panic capture were subsequently implemented and tested as described in the current update above. Legacy pathname operations did not resolve the fresh namespace mount in that initial fixture. This remains a QEMU-only experiment, not a production desktop handoff or physical panic writer. Initial test-only payload: `build/hardware/guard-journal-publish-pair-v5-20261105/`.

The experimental guarded repair now requires its original checker controller to consume a completed, drained, clean FAT-check result and revalidate the FAT profile under the retained disk reservation before obtaining the preparation adapter. A disposable KVM fixture passed the pending transaction, refused a missing admission marker, and repaired a deliberately dirty ext2 filesystem through verification and guard completion. This handoff remains restricted to the test build; it does not yet provide production mount authority or bind the panic journal. KVM is available outside the workspace sandbox, where `/dev/kvm` is visible; the sandbox itself hides that device. Use the required access for KVM tests rather than interpreting the sandbox view as host capability.

An explicit fixture-only option now requests a guest reset after successful guarded repair and verified clean-record completion. In one KVM process, a dirty private disk completed the repair, issued the reset, passed through EFI and reached normal boot; an injected completion failure did not request reset and the guarded EFI continued to block normal boot. The full disk range and independent filesystem checks still ran. This is not enabled in production, does not implement panic or hang reset, and does not prove physical reset or power-loss behavior.

The automatic-repair path independently classifies the identity-bound ext2 superblock while the data partition remains reserved: only `NeedsCheck` enters the repair transaction, a clean filesystem stays in diagnostics, and unsupported or invalid geometry is refused. Disposable KVM runs covered clean and unsupported filesystems with unchanged disk hashes, and a compatible dirty 4 KiB filesystem through repair, verification and guest-initiated normal reboot.

An earlier isolated `BROOK_SSD_AUTO_RECOVERY` candidate used that transaction without the QEMU-only write/fault hooks. It required the guard-check boot, exact configured disk identity, clean FAT checker completion, matching guard records, dirty supported ext2, preen, a separate clean verification, and durable guard completion before one reset attempt. At that stage a pending guard blocked an interrupted attempt from repeating; the bounded retry described above supersedes that behavior. On a private KVM disk with an identity-bound data-inspecting EFI loader, dirty data selected recovery without F5, was repaired and verified, and rebooted to normal; a clean disk remained unchanged and a modified FAT checker was refused. Host checker/repair session tests passed. This is a build candidate only: the physical loader inventory/migration, reviewed matched recovery initrd and physical validation remain. One separate concurrent QEMU final boot timed out; the subsequent standalone automatic-dispatch run passed its full boot and disk checks.

`prepare_guard_check_pair.py --automatic --e2fsck <pinned-checker>` now creates an identity-bound automatic-recovery pair, verifies the kernel build options and both checker hashes, and reads back the initrd files. An optional `BROOK_BUILD_BOOT_INVENTORY` EFI build records UEFI boot variables to a new `RECOVERY/BOOTVARS.TXT` without changing firmware variables or overwriting an existing report, then continues normal boot. A disposable KVM SATA disk booted twice, preserved the first report, and decoded its boot order and current entry. The host decoder flags missing or malformed referenced options; inventory data can contain private firmware load-option details. At the initial inventory, the SSD EFI directory listed `BOOTX64.EFI` and `BROOKF5.EFI`, but that does not establish the firmware boot order or all devices. Brook's FAT rename implementation unlinks an existing target before renaming, so a replacement of the existing default loader has an interruption window. Do not enable automatic repair until all potential boot paths and a safe migration/recovery procedure have been established.

Ian subsequently booted `BROOKINV.EFI`; boot `cf4b013a47334fe5afbd7a7a34dde6d2` is reachable and reports the existing `dell-pch-inspect-20261105` payload. Boot0000 is a Windows entry outside the order. The SSD entry contains two complete device paths in its FilePathList; the host decoder now preserves them separately. Local uncommitted recovery work reserves the AHCI panic gate before halting peers, allowing an in-flight operation to relinquish its DMA buffer; a stuck owner remains bounded and capture is skipped. Disposable TCG tests passed journal capture twice, exception capture and a deliberately permanently busy gate with unchanged disk and reset. A startup-I/O contention integration test remains unproven. Separately, a panic-halt owner that faults can now invoke the armed reset without waiting for a halted peer; a disposable guarded KVM test injected #UD after capture, observed `PANIC_OWNER_EXCEPTION` and reset, and independently verified the preserved journal. These changes have not been deployed to the Dell.

Follow-up disposable tests exercised a peer #UD against a different panic-halt owner: the peer parked without reset or journal mutation (`build/hardware/guard-panic-peer-fault-20261105/`). A Dell-initrd QEMU startup script with an appended guest `panic` captured the exact reason, reset, and retrieved the same packet over emulated USB before filesystem repair (`build/hardware/guard-dell-startup-panic-serial-fix-20261105/`). A prior run showed concurrent ordinary serial output garbling the panic header; normal character output now checks the panic flag even when already inside its output lock. The successful run had a readable header, though individual race-window bytes remain possible and the run did not demonstrate a busy-to-panic AHCI handoff.

An additional KVM-only, test-hook build forced a real AHCI data writer to hold the gate after its write completed until the startup panic requested ownership. The run observed `PANIC_CONTENTION_WRITER_HELD`, `PANIC_DISK_RESERVE_WAIT`, `PANIC_DISK_RESERVE_READY`, crash capture, reset, identical packet retrieval over emulated USB, and guarded repair (`build/hardware/guard-dell-ahci-contention-retest-20261105/`). The hook requires an explicit build option, KVM, the QEMU AHCI identity and fw_cfg selector; the recovery pair preparer rejects it in both the build cache and compile flags. This establishes the instrumented handoff, not arbitrary physical disk failures or power-loss durability. The test kernel and fixture must never be deployed.

Prepared fresh private physical-profile images from the current sources: guarded desktop `build/hardware/dell-guarded-desktop-panic-v2-20261105/` and restricted USB recovery `build/hardware/dell-guard-recovery-panic-v2-20261105/`. A QEMU fixture using the same kernels and refreshed desktop initrd, with selectors rewritten for its own disk and synthetic application services, captured a guest startup panic, reset and retrieved the packet through emulated USB before repair (`build/hardware/guard-dell-pair-v2-exact-modules-20261105/`). Current Dell boot `cf4b013a47334fe5afbd7a7a34dde6d2` still reports the expected controller and drive; its read-only sectors 1, 2 and 526338 hash identically to the earlier reviewed snapshot, including the ext2 UUID. This is not a fresh check of the full GPT array or a filesystem check. Neither candidate has been staged or activated: the SSD boot entry does not specify a filename, existing explicit F5 and inventory entries use separate loaders, and safe migration must account for those paths without losing the working recovery route.

Host tests and private QEMU boots checked valid alternate, missing selector and corrupt initrd (`build/hardware/guard-alt-recovery-qemu-20261105/`). A separate create-only `BROOKG2.EFI` staging helper passed host and QEMU readback/FAT checks (`guard-alt-efi-stage-qemu-20261105.log`). Ian subsequently explicitly authorized staging and making the new loader default. On boot `cf4b013a47334fe5afbd7a7a34dde6d2`, create-only jobs `55ac47063e5a4c8d90b75557f8fcfd1b` and `bb1d5f05c00a49c8a87d808ff861da3a` staged the pair and EFI, respectively, with exit zero; independent job `f2b96ec90e7942d7a0700b87729a8a41` confirmed all four hashes and the original default and F5 hashes. The undeployed opt-in GPU VT-d diagnostic now samples the capability register and, only if a protected-memory region is supported, the protected-memory enable/status register. Intel VT-d specifies that protected memory is distinct from address translation; the raw diagnostic is not DMA admission or proof of exclusive ownership. Its host probe test and normal kernel build passed; the new diagnostic is not on the Dell.

The alternate-loader QEMU regression now also removes both recovery selectors and observes no kernel boot for 15 seconds (`build/hardware/guard-alt-recovery-all-invalid-qemu-20261105/`). Disposable AHCI panic capture: BROOK_AHCI_PANIC_TEST is a separate non-production build that requires explicit QEMU fw_cfg, an exact 64 MiB QEMU SATA disk identity and an unpartitioned scratch disk. After panic or #UD it acquires the panic gate without waiting, writes the journal through bounded AHCI polling and flush, reads it back, and then exercises the QEMU-only reset. TCG/OVMF tests independently decoded disk contents and matched PANIC_HEX for two sequential captures and an exception. Missing marker, wrong serial, corrupt journal and a simulated busy gate left the scratch disk untouched. This does not authorize a physical disk, map a preallocated FAT file, detect every damaged device, prove power-loss durability, or implement production reset/inhibition.

AHCI capture prerequisite: normal command/DMA operations now enter an atomic gate under their existing mutex. A panic claimant may acquire the idle gate without waiting and retain it until reboot; it must skip capture when ordinary I/O owns it. Host race tests pass; a disposable QEMU boot mounted an identity-bound SATA fixture and wrote, synced and independently read back a file. A claimant and disk writer now exist only in the separate disposable build described above; no physical hardware was changed.

Crash capture preparation: the structured packet is available in boot-lifetime static memory. A two-slot fixed-sector journal stores up to 64 KiB per capture with CRC, data-first flush/readback and header-last publication; host fault injection covers read, partial write and flush failures while preserving the prior slot. A host test round-trips an actual headless panic packet through it. This journal is not connected to a device, the filesystem, or physical storage; its memory-disk tests do not prove SSD durability. AHCI uses scheduler-aware locking and shared DMA, so a panic-safe ownership and I/O path remains necessary before deployment.

Panic-reset experiment: a QEMU-fw_cfg-only test path waits one second after a panic dump and issues the selected reset once; it is disabled on the Dell. Disposable TCG/OVMF runs passed a deliberate panic, an unarmed control, a #UD exception and an actual second boot. Both panic and exception emitted PANIC_HEX. The fixture kernel and its optional audio module have different ABI versions; the module was rejected and was not involved in these tests. The test does not establish physical timing, data integrity, hang recovery, durable capture, reset inhibition or reboot-loop prevention.

## Project and working relationship

Brook is Ian Norris's hobby x86-64 operating system, built from scratch in C++ with Clang/LLVM. It boots with UEFI, supports SMP and loadable drivers, has a native desktop with a Wayland compositor, and implements a growing Linux syscall ABI so unmodified Linux applications and Nix closures can run. This is a custom OS, not a Linux distribution.

The development host is Linux with a pinned Nix environment. The repository inspected here is `/data/Programming/Codex/Brook`. Its README documents `nix-shell`, `./scripts/build.sh Release` and the broader `build_all.sh`; select the smallest relevant target after consulting the task's existing notes. Do not run the full image and application pipeline merely to establish that the handover works.

Ian values clean architecture, usable applications, reproducible fresh builds and practical progress. He actively tests milestones and supplies hardware observations. He has repeatedly requested bounded investigations and discouraged diminishing returns. Preserve the reasons behind prior decisions, distinguish provisional experiments from accepted defaults, and avoid rebuilding a private collection of undocumented helpers.

## Acceptance for the recovery milestone

The recovery pair and required diagnostic tools are published to the admitted SSD boot partition with identity verification, space checks, ordered write/flush/readback and a retained loader backup. The F5-capable loader can select that verified recovery pair, and the normal desktop path still boots. Ian can launch local diagnostics without a functioning host connection. While the bridge is up, the host can also invoke the guest diagnostic and retrieve its result. Reports distinguish host reachability, guest interface/network status, bridge failure and unknown state. A guest loopback reply covers only the guest-side path. USB recovery remains available.

The existing host-side `scripts/probe_hardware_link.py` checks route, ping, neighbor state and a framed hardware-capabilities response at a specified endpoint. Its failures do not distinguish a guest hang from link loss or a panic. Combine that evidence with the guest-local diagnostic; do not treat a successful TCP connection as a healthy bridge.

Use the existing disposable-image evidence for already tested loader and image behavior. Exercise the integrated publisher and any newly introduced failure paths. Physical acceptance should establish the actual SSD recovery selection, tool launch and retained normal boot. Preserve the expected guarantees and state their limits; arbitrary power-loss tolerance is not established by stopping QEMU.

The watchdog is a separate follow-up unless Ian changes the milestone. Its current design requires explicit arming for the current boot, heartbeats through the actual bridge, three-minute expiry, observable status, inhibition during repair/update/flush/shutdown, and no automatic rearm loop after restart. It cannot guarantee recovery from a completely wedged kernel.

## Established capabilities and important limits

- The native QEMU development path supports a substantial Linux application stack, browsers, Wine/Proton and VirGL/Venus experiments. Virtual GPU successes do not establish a physical Intel graphics driver.
- Steam authentication, library operations and native64 Stardew gameplay/save/reload have prior successful evidence in QEMU, including Ian's gameplay acceptance. Preserve those results. Dell Steam reliability is a separate unresolved question.
- Rootless Xwayland and Brook's private XWM already exist. Individual Steam windows have rendered in native desktop windows, with focus, geometry and close controls. Broad Dell acceptance remains incomplete. Do not restart the architecture from nested Xephyr; keep nested X as a diagnostic fallback.
- The missing Xwayland `setitimer` interface is real. `-dumbSched` suppresses its repeated unsupported calls, but the comparisons did not establish a Steam performance or Dell stability improvement. Keep that conclusion narrow.
- The Broadwell work includes guarded forcewake observations, command/context preparation, mapping/lifetime gates and simulated submission machinery. It does not yet establish a working physical GPU execution backend.
- Network/bridge loss and recurrent dirty filesystems have occurred. A missing bridge is not proof of a guest crash; use local diagnostics and the documented recovery path. Do not replay uncertain writes or restart jobs solely after a timeout.
